textual_basis: At 762c-762d, the Athenian says officials and field-wardens should live for the two years with common meals in each place, where all must make their diet together. Anyone absent from the mess for any day, or sleeping away any night, unless assigned by officials or compelled by necessity, is to be denounced by the five, posted in the marketplace as having dissolved the guard, reproached by the constitution as betraying his part, and punished with blows by whoever meets him and wishes to punish without penalty. If one of the officials does the same, all sixty must attend to it, and whoever knows or hears but does not prosecute is subject to the same laws with greater penalty than the young and is dishonored from all offices over the young. Law-guardians are to be exact overseers so that such things either do not occur or receive fitting justice.
limits: This records discipline for common meals and guard desertion. It does not include the broader principle that service precedes rule.

The first service is to the laws, since this is service to the gods; next, the young always serve elders and those who have lived honorably. After this, anyone who has become a field-warden must have tasted the humble and resource-poor daily life for the two years. Once the twelve are enrolled and join the five, they should deliberate that, like household servants, they will not have other servants or slaves for themselves, nor use attendants from farmers and villagers for their private services, except for public matters; otherwise they must live serving and being served by themselves.

observation: For choral musical play involving boys, men, and girls in dances and order, one official at least forty years old is sufficient; for solo song, one official at least thirty is sufficient to introduce competitors and judge distinctions. textual_basis: At 764e-765a, the Athenian says they must first choose officials for the play of choruses of boys, men, and female children in dances and the whole musical order. One official is sufficient for these if he is not less than forty years old. One official is also sufficient for solo song, not less than thirty years old, to be introducer and to give adequate distinction to competitors. For choosing the official and arranger of choruses, those who have a friendly disposition toward such matters are to go to the gathering and are liable to a fine if they do not, with the law-guardians as judges; for others, if they do not wish to attend, there is no compulsion.
limits: This records the age and attendance rules through 765a. It does not cover the remaining voting procedure that follows after the cited marker.
review_status: accepted
```

A successor must understand how to guard and correct the laws so that the constitution and civic order become better rather than worse over time."
textual_basis: "At 769d, the Athenian asks whether this is not also the legislator's wish: first to write the laws sufficiently according to possible precision, then, as time advances and practical tests occur, not to be so foolish as to ignore that many things must necessarily be left out and that someone following must correct them. The stated aim is that the constitution and order around the founded city should become in no way worse but always better at 769e. He then asks whether anyone with a device for this, in deed and words, could teach another how to understand guarding and correcting laws more or less, and Clinias answers through 770b that they should try to say it if they can."
limits: This records the legislative successor-and-correction requirement. It does not identify the substantive standard for correction stated afterward.

observation: After the offices report to the law-guardians and the laws are completed, the enacted laws are to stand immovable. Voluntary alteration is forbidden; if necessity ever compels a change, every office, the whole people, and all divine oracles must agree, while a single objector preserves the existing law.
textual_basis: At 772c-772d, the Athenian says all the offices will meet with the law-guardians and state what each office has found by experience and inquiry, until the laws for that office seem sufficiently established. The laws so set are to remain immovable. No one may willingly move them. If some necessity appears, all offices, the whole people, and the oracles of the gods must be consulted together. If everyone agrees, the law may be changed; if anyone opposes, the opposing side prevails according to law.
limits: This records the finalization and amendment threshold for office laws. It does not include the following transition into marriage law.
review_status: accepted

observation: Marriage legislation begins with an age window and a demand for a preluding argument. A man who has found the partner suitable for shared child-producing should marry after twenty-five and before thirty-five, but he must first hear how to search for what is fitting and harmonious, since each law ought to have its own prelude.
textual_basis: At 772d-772e, the Athenian says that when a man is twenty-five and has observed and been observed by others, he should marry after finding the woman who is fitting and harmonious for partnership in generation. Everyone should marry before age thirty-five. First, however, he must hear how to seek what is fitting and harmonious, because, as Clinias says, each law must have its own proper prelude.

english_gloss: marriages, rich, poor, equals, city, characters, temperate, sharper
observation: "The marriage prelude counsels citizens to marry for the city's benefit rather than private pleasure: those who are equal should prefer the poorer household over the richer, and temperamental opposites should be paired so that wealth and character do not grow uneven through attraction to the similar."
textual_basis: At 773a-773b, the Athenian says the child of reputable people should not flee from marriages with poor people or eagerly pursue marriages with rich people. Other things being equal, one should prefer the lower estate, because this helps both city and households. A bold and quick character should seek kin from more orderly parents, while the opposite nature should go toward the opposite. He explains that everyone is naturally drawn to similar marriage, but the whole city becomes uneven in wealth and character when citizens marry for what pleases themselves rather than what benefits the city.
limits: This records the balancing advice in the marriage prelude. It does not state the later distinction between persuasion and written compulsion.
review_status: accepted
```

```yaml
observation_id: obs_laws_0730

greek_terms:
  - πόλις
english_gloss: law, ridiculous, become angry, be mixed, city, wealth, characters, songs
observation: The proposed marriage balance is explicitly treated as unsuitable for blunt written coercion. Since a law forbidding rich-rich matches or forcing temperament mixing would seem ridiculous and anger citizens, the city should pursue the needed mixture through persuasion, charm, and shame rather than written compulsion.
textual_basis: At 773c-773e, the Athenian says a written law telling the wealthy not to marry into wealthy households, or compelling the quick to marry the slow and the slow the quick, would be ridiculous to many people and would cause anger. Yet the city must be mixed like a cup in which a raging liquid becomes a moderate and good drink when mixed with the sober god. Because almost no one can see that this applies to child-generation, lawgiving should leave such matters to songs and try to charm each person into valuing balanced children over money, while shaming money-focused marriage.
limits: This records the method distinction for marriage balancing. It does not include the later penalties for refusing marriage altogether.
review_status: accepted
```

```yaml
observation_id: obs_laws_0731
source_work: Laws

greek_terms:
  - τριάκοντα
  - Ἥρας
  - νεωτέρων
english_gloss: marriage, five, thirty, penalty, Hera, treasurers, dishonor, younger people
observation: After the marriage preludes, a man still unmarried at thirty-five is treated as alien to civic sharing. He pays annual fines by property class dedicated to Hera, faces dishonor from younger people, and loses ordinary authority over the young when he attempts to punish them.
textual_basis: "At 774a-774b, the Athenian sets the written law after the marriage preludes: whoever does not obey and remains apart from the city, unmarried at age thirty-five, must pay annual penalties according to property class, with the proceeds sacred to Hera. The treasurers of Hera are liable for the full amount if they fail to collect. The unmarried man is also to suffer dishonor from younger people, and none of the young should obey him. If he tries to punish anyone, everyone must aid the wronged person, and any bystander who fails to help is called cowardly and base by law."
limits: This records the fines, dedication, collection liability, and civic dishonor for remaining unmarried. It does not include the following rules about dowries and wedding expenses.
review_status: accepted
```

Anyone giving or receiving more than the class-scaled clothing allowance must owe the same amount again to the public, while what was given or received is sacred to Hera and Zeus and is collected by their treasurers.

  - νύμφην
  - νυμφίον
english_gloss: be drunk, Dionysia, bride, bridegroom, be sensible, generation, sowing, god
observation: Drunkenness is excluded from serious marriage, especially at the beginning of procreation. Bride and groom should be most sound-minded at this life transition because conception from bodies loosened by drink is said to produce unstable, unjust, and crooked offspring, while the beginning and the god in human affairs preserve what is rightly honored.
textual_basis: At 775b-775e, the Athenian says drunkenness is generally improper except at Dionysiac festivals and unsafe around marriage. Bride and bridegroom should be especially sensible while undergoing a major change of life and when it is not clear which night or day generation occurs. He says that generation should not occur from bodies dissolved by drunkenness, because the one sown should be compact, steady, and quiet, whereas a drunk sower produces something wandering, untrustworthy, and not straight in character or body. Therefore the procreator must be careful not to implant disease, hubris, or injustice, especially on the day and night of conception; the beginning and the god among humans preserve everything when properly honored.
limits: This records the sobriety rule and generative rationale through 775e. It does not include later pregnancy or household regulations.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: "At 777c-777d, the Athenian points to repeated Messenian revolts, cities with many household servants from one language, and Italian cases involving thefts and sufferings. He says these make one perplexed about what to do, but two devices remain: keep those who will serve from being fellow-countrymen and make them as discordant in speech as possible; also rear them correctly, not merely for their sake but more for the masters' sake, by avoiding outrage and injustice toward household servants."
limits: This records the examples and the two stated management devices through 777d. It does not include the continuation about being untainted in slave-related practices.
review_status: accepted

observation: The lawgiver is said to reason wrongly if he legislates public and common conduct while leaving necessary private matters unordered and unlegislated. The principle introduces the claim that newlyweds too must have an ordered way of life rather than unrestricted daily freedom.
textual_basis: At 780a, the Athenian criticizes anyone who gives cities laws for public and common life but thinks the necessary private matters need not be regulated, leaving each person free to live each day as he wishes and leaving private matters unlegislated. He says such a person is wrong to expect citizens to live by laws in common and public matters, and then introduces the requirement concerning newlyweds.
limits: This records the public-private legislation principle at 780a. It does not include the historical account of common meals that follows.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 780b-780c, the Athenian says the newlyweds must make their way of life in common meals no less than in the period before marriage. He then describes the first appearance of this practice in the addressees' regions as wondrous, likely legislated by war or another force of equal power among people constrained by fewness and difficulty. After they tasted and were compelled to use common meals, the legal custom seemed to make a great difference for preservation and became established among them.

textual_basis: At 780c-780d, after noting that common meals once seemed wondrous and fearful to impose but are now easier to legislate, the Athenian says the next thing would be rightly natural if it came to be, yet now exists nowhere and makes the legislator seem nearly to be doing futile work. When Clinias asks why he hesitates, the Athenian answers that everything in a city sharing in order and law produces goods, while unordered or badly ordered things dissolve many other well-ordered things.

The lawgiver is said to have yielded wrongly in leaving this difficult matter alone, with many matters worse than they would be under laws.
textual_basis: At 780e-781a, the Athenian tells Clinias and Megillus that the common meals for men are well and wondrously established by a kind of divine necessity. He then contrasts the case of women, saying the practice of their common meals has not rightly been left unlegislated and has not come into the light. He adds that because the female part is more hidden and hard to manage, the lawgiver wrongly yielded and left it alone, and that many matters have slipped away which would be much better if they had obtained laws.
limits: This records the contrast between men's and women's common meals and the charge of legislative omission. It does not rely on the continuation after 781a.

textual_basis: At 782e, the speaker says all human things depend on threefold need and desire, through which virtue or its opposite comes about depending on how people are led. observation: The period for child-production and its supervision is limited to ten years when generation flows well. If a couple remains childless during that period, separation is to be decided jointly with relatives and the ruling women according to what is fitting for both parties.
textual_basis: At 784b, the Athenian says child-making and the guarding of those producing children should last ten years and no longer, whenever there is a good flow of generation. If some couples are childless by that time, they are to separate after common deliberation with relatives and the ruling women about what is advantageous for each.
limits: This records the time limit and infertility separation rule. It does not include the law-guardian arbitration for disputes.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 784c, the Athenian says that if a dispute arises about what is fitting for either party, they should choose ten law-guardians and abide by what those guardians assign. The women supervisors enter the houses of the young, sometimes admonishing and sometimes threatening, to stop error and ignorance. If they cannot, they go to the law-guardians; if the law-guardians also cannot restrain the matter, they announce it to the public.

textual_basis: At 784d, the Athenian says the inscribed man is dishonored unless he defeats in court those who registered him. He may not go to weddings or to the completion rites of children; if he goes, anyone who wishes may punish him with blows without liability. The same legal rules apply concerning a woman, including women's outings, honors, and attendance at weddings and children's birthdays if she is inscribed and fails to win her case.

observation: The civic register distinguishes the living from those who have died and sets age thresholds for marriage, office, and military service. Girls marry from sixteen to twenty, men from thirty to thirty-five, women enter offices at forty and men at thirty, and men's military service runs from twenty to sixty, with women's military use determined after childbearing.
textual_basis: At 785b, the Athenian says those still living should be written nearby in the phratry record, while those departing life should be erased. He sets the limit of marriage for a girl from sixteen to twenty years at the longest, and for a young man from thirty to thirty-five. For offices, a woman is to be forty and a man thirty. For war, a man serves from twenty to sixty; a woman is to be used for military needs, if such use seems required, after she has borne children.
limits: This records the age thresholds stated at 785b. It does not specify the later rules for nurture and education.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: Once male and female children have been born, nurture and education are necessary topics, but the speaker treats them as better handled by teaching and admonition than by written law. Private household details are too small and frequent for penalties, yet if left to pleasure, pain, and desire they produce diverse civic characters and habituate lawbreaking.
textual_basis: At 788a-788b, the Athenian says that after children of both sexes have been born, it is most correct to speak next of nurture and education. These cannot be left wholly unspoken, but when spoken they resemble teaching and admonition more than laws. Many small private household matters are not visible to everyone and are easily shaped against the legislator's advice by each person's pain, pleasure, and desire, producing varied and unlike citizen characters. Making penal laws for such small and frequent things would be improper and ugly, and would corrupt written laws by habituating people to lawbreaking in small matters.
limits: This records the difficulty of legislating household nurture. It does not yet state the examples introduced in the following passage.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: bodies, finest, children, first, sprout, growth, exercises, nourishment, mothers, embryos
observation: The first bodily rule links beauty to straight early growth and proportional exercise. Because the earliest growth of a living thing is greatest, abundant nourishment without many proportionate motions produces bodily evils; the need for exercise therefore applies even before birth to children being nourished inside their mothers.
textual_basis: At 788d-789a, the Athenian says the simplest point about the finest bodies is that children should grow straight from youth. He notes that the first sprout of every living thing grows most and fastest, and that great growth without many proportionate exercises produces countless bodily evils. Therefore bodies need the most exercise when the most nourishment is added. When Clinias asks whether this means assigning many exercises to newborns, the Athenian says not at all, but even earlier, to those nourished inside their mothers, identifying the unborn children.
limits: This records the growth-and-exercise argument. It does not include the later comparison to animal training.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The causal explanation is that both infant distress and Bacchic disturbance involve fear-affections from a bad condition of soul. External shaking and motion overcome the inner fearful and manic motion, producing calm and quiet in the soul; for children this brings sleep, and for awake dancers with divine rites it replaces manic conditions with sound-minded ones.
textual_basis: At 791a, the Athenian speaker identifies both conditions as fears, says an externally supplied shaking overpowers the inner fearful and manic motion, and describes the resulting calm and quiet in the soul. The same marker distinguishes the outcome for sleepers from the outcome for awake dancers and flute-accompanied participants in rites.
limits: This records the explanation given within 791a. It does not extend to the later summary beyond the next marker.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The passage distinguishes reducing infant distress from supplying many pleasures. A difficult and ungentle person is associated with lamentation, and minimizing pain, fears, and every grief during the three years is proposed as making the reared soul more cheerful and gentle; when Cleinias adds many pleasures, the Athenian rejects that as the greatest corruption because it occurs at the beginning of nurture.
textual_basis: At 792b-792c, the Athenian asks whether a difficult person who is not gentle is usually too full of lamentation and wailing for a good person. He then asks whether every device during the three years that makes the child use as little pain, fear, and grief as possible would make the reared soul more cheerful and gentle. Cleinias answers by adding many pleasures, but at 792c the Athenian says he will no longer follow him and calls such action the greatest corruption, since it happens at the beginning of nurture.
limits: This records the contrast between distress reduction and pleasure provision. It does not include the completed middle doctrine stated at the next marker.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The harmless left-right division used with lyre and plectrum is treated as a bad model for other activities. Scythian archery and other practices show that both sides can be trained, so making left capacities weaker than right is described as contrary to nature.
textual_basis: At 794e-795a, the Athenian allows that some tasks are not greatly affected by left-right specialization, then calls it foolish to extend those examples to other work. He cites Scythian bow use and further examples such as chariot-driving to show that making left capacities weaker than right is contrary to nature.
limits: This records the examples used to reject generalized hand bias. It does not yet cover the special importance of this training for war with weapons.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: children's games, laws, stable, play, games, innovated, young, characters, old, new
observation: The account makes children's games decisive for legal stability. If the young always play the same games in the same ways, serious laws remain quietly in place; if games and bodily styles are constantly innovated, the young's characters shift unnoticed, the old becomes dishonored, and the new becomes honored.
textual_basis: At 797a-797c, the Athenian says it is strange and unfamiliar but necessary to state that in every city the whole class of children's games is ignored, although it is most authoritative for whether established laws are stable. When games are ordered so that the same children play the same games in the same ways and enjoy the same playthings, serious laws remain calmly. But when the games are moved, innovated, and always changed, and the young do not consistently call the same things graceful in bodily shapes or other equipment, someone who always introduces something new in shapes, colors, and similar matters is wrongly honored; this secretly changes young characters, dishonors the old, and honors the new.
limits: This records the children's-game argument through the old-new contrast. It does not include the later body-and-soul habit analogy.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The defense of old custom treats change as dangerous except in bad things and uses bodily habituation as the model. Bodies become healthy and pleased by familiar foods, drinks, and exercises but are disturbed by dietary change; likewise, souls raised under long-unchanged laws come to revere and fear moving anything established, so the legislator must devise a way to make that stability occur.
textual_basis: "At 797d-798b, Clinias identifies the claim as criticism of despising antiquity. The Athenian says change is very dangerous in almost all things except evils, including seasons, winds, bodily diets, and souls. He compares bodies accustomed to foods, drinks, and exercises: after initial disturbance they grow flesh fitted to that diet and live best with familiar things, but when forced to change a reputable diet they are shaken by diseases until the old nourishment restores habit. The same must be thought about human understandings and souls. People reared under laws that by divine fortune remain unmoved for long times, with no memory or report that they were ever otherwise, revere and fear changing anything established. The legislator must find a device for producing this in the city."
limits: This records the habit analogy and legislator's problem. It does not yet explain how changing children's games threatens future laws.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: games, innovating, men, life, practices, laws, characters, praise, blame, shifts
observation: Adults wrongly treat changes in children's games as mere play, but innovation in games makes children become different adults. Those adults then seek a different life, practices, and laws; the gravest changes are those that repeatedly shift judgments of praise and blame concerning character.
textual_basis: At 798c-798d, the Athenian says people think moving children's games is really only play and does no serious harm, so they do not turn it back but follow and yield. They fail to calculate that children who innovate in games must become different men from the earlier children, and as different adults they seek another life, then desire different practices and laws, after which the great civic evil arrives. Smaller changes in shapes may produce lesser harms, but frequent shifts in praise and blame concerning characters are the greatest and need the most caution.
limits: This records the causal chain from play innovation to legal change and character judgment shifts. It does not include the specific musical remedy introduced next.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: "Because rhythm and music are imitations of better and worse characters, the city must prevent children from desiring different dance and melody models or being lured by varied pleasures. The proposed technique is Egyptian-style consecration: fix dances, songs, festivals, gods, and appropriate hymns before they enter ordinary innovation."
textual_basis: "At 798e-799a, Clinias agrees that rhythm and all music are imitations of better and worse characters. The Athenian says every device must be devised so that children do not desire to touch other imitations in dances or melodies and so that no one persuades them by bringing varied pleasures. He asks whether there is any better art for this than the Egyptians' practice: consecrating every dance and every melody, first arranging the annual festivals, determining for which gods, children of gods, and daimons they must occur and at what times, and then determining which song should be sung over each sacrifice and with which choruses each occasion should be honored."
limits: This records the opening Egyptian-style musical remedy through 799a. It does not include the further institutional ratification after this marker.
review_status: accepted
```

If the excluded person does not willingly withdraw, anyone who wishes may bring impiety suits against him for life.

The present case must be handled similarly because a strange argument about laws has arisen. They should not lightly claim immediate clarity about such great matters, but should give it time and confirm it after sufficient inquiry. To avoid being blocked from completing the next order of laws, they proceed toward the end, hoping the whole passage may later reveal the current perplexity.

observation: "If citizens must hear lamenting songs, the proper setting is exceptional and funeral-like: inauspicious days, hired outside singers, and opposite dress from festive crowns and gold. The first musical law therefore requires auspicious speech."
textual_basis: At 800e-801a, the Athenian says that if citizens ever must listen to such pity-inducing songs, it should be on unclean and inauspicious days and should use hired choruses of singers from outside, like those who accompany the dead with a Carian sort of muse. Such songs should also have appropriate funeral dress, not crowns or gold adornment but the opposite. He then asks that this be granted, and Clinias says the law wins by every vote. The Athenian identifies auspicious speech as the first law of music.
limits: This records the exception for lament and the first music-law rule. It does not include the subsequent rules about prayers and poets.
review_status: accepted
```

The Athenian asks whether, if women do not share the whole of life in common with men, it is necessary for them to have some separate order; Clinias agrees, and the Athenian begins to compare that separate order with the community now being prescribed.
textual_basis: At 805d, after restating shared participation, the Athenian asks whether women who do not share all of life in common with men must have a different order of their own. Clinias answers that this is necessary, and the Athenian then frames a comparison between that community and the one now being prescribed.
limits: This records the order-choice question and agreement at 805d. It does not include the later comparative alternatives outside the assigned marker.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 810b-810c, after the literacy rule the speaker turns to poets' unaccompanied lessons set in writing, some with meters and some without rhythmic divisions. He describes writings stated only according to speech, lacking rhythm and harmony, as risky writings left by many such people, and asks the law-guardians what they should use and what command the lawgiver could rightly set down.

observation: The curriculum problem is framed around the huge range of poetry in different meters, some serious and some comic. Since every poet says many fine things and many contrary things, making children widely learned by memorizing whole poets or selected anthologies is dangerous unless the law-guardian has a standard for what to allow and forbid.
textual_basis: At 810e-811c, the Athenian says there are many poets in hexameter, trimeter, and every meter, some directed toward seriousness and others toward laughter. Many advisers say the correctly educated should become widely learned by memorizing whole poets, while others select summaries and complete speeches from all poets and require memorization for wisdom through wide experience and learning. He answers that each of these poets says many things well and many things in the opposite way, so such wide learning brings danger for children. Clinias asks what model the law-guardian should look to when allowing or preventing what the young learn.
limits: This records the curricular danger and need for a law-guardian selection standard. It does not yet state the proposed model.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The proposed model for grammar education is the very discourse the speakers have carried on since morning, treated as poetry-like and divinely inspired enough for young listeners. Teachers must teach these speeches and similar allied writings, and only teachers who learn and praise them should be used as educational collaborators.
textual_basis: At 811d-812a, the Athenian says he is pleased when he looks at the collected speeches they have made since morning and judges them, among most speeches in poetry or prose that he knows, to be most moderate and most fitting for young people to hear. He says he cannot offer the law-guardian and educator a better model than to tell teachers to teach these things to children, along with writings or unwritten sayings from poets or prose that are akin to them. Teachers themselves must be compelled first to learn and praise them; teachers who do not approve should not be used, while those who join in praise should receive the young for teaching and education.
limits: This records the model for letters and grammar instruction. It does not include the later citharist rules.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 812b-812c, the Athenian moves from the letter-teacher to the citharist and recalls the earlier rule. The sixty-year-old singers of Dionysus should be especially perceptive about rhythms and the structures of harmonies, so that they can choose the good and badly imitated song-imitation when an affection occurs in the soul. They are to reject one kind, bring the other into public, hymn it, and sing it as a charm over the souls of the young, calling each toward the acquisition of virtue by following through the imitations.

observation: Lyre instruction is restricted to clarity and matching notes, not complex heterophony and ornamental rhythmic variation. Because students must grasp the useful part of music quickly within three years and already have many necessary studies, contrary combinations that confuse learning should not be introduced.
textual_basis: At 812d-812e, the Athenian says the citharist and student should use the notes of the lyre for the sake of clarity of the strings, giving note against note. They should not introduce heterophony and variety, with strings sending one melody while the poet-composer makes another, nor dense against sparse, quick against slow, high against low, concordant and antiphonal effects, or many rhythmic ornaments fitted to lyre notes. Such things should not be offered to those who must quickly grasp the useful part of music in three years, because opposites disturbing one another make learning difficult while the young need to be as teachable as possible.
limits: This records the technical limits on music instruction. It does not include the festival consecration and music-officer handoff.
review_status: accepted
```

When Clinias asks how an older man can manage so much, the Athenian says the law has given and will give him the power to take as assistants whichever male and female citizens he wants. He will know whom to choose and will not want to fail, recognizing the greatness of the office and that when the young are well reared everything sails rightly."

observation: Military gymnastics requires public teachers paid by the city and students of both sexes. Boys, men, girls, and women should learn armed dance, combat, formation, handling arms, tactical movement, marching, encampment, and riding-related subjects, so that women can help guard children and the city when the whole citizen force is away or when the city itself is attacked.
textual_basis: "At 813e-814b, the Athenian lists bodily exercises around war: archery, throwing, peltast training, every kind of fighting in arms, tactical passages, marching and encampment, and horsemanship-related studies. There must be public teachers for all these, paid by the city, and the city's boys and men, girls and women, must be students of them. Girls while still girls should practice every armed dance and battle, and as women should be attached to formations, placing and taking up arms. This is useful if the entire force must leave the city on campaign and others must guard the children and city, or if enemies, barbarian or Greek, force battle over the city itself. The passage criticizes shameful female upbringing that would leave women unable to fight for children and instead rushing to shrines."
limits: This records the public military-training curriculum and the reason for including women. It does not include the formal law and wrestling qualification that follow.
review_status: accepted

observation: The account classifies bodily motion, most of which is called dance, into imitations of fine and ugly bodies, with serious dance split into warlike and peaceful forms. The warlike form is pyrrhic, imitating avoidance and attack, while Bacchic and related ritual imitations are set apart as neither civic warlike nor civic peaceful dance.
textual_basis: "At 814e-815c, the Athenian says most bodily motion may rightly be called dance and should be thought to have two kinds: one imitating finer bodies toward dignity and another uglier bodies toward baseness, with further divisions of the base and serious. The serious kind includes a warlike dance involving noble bodies and courageous soul in violent labors and a peaceful dance in good fortune. The warlike dance is rightly called pyrrhic, imitating precautions against blows and missiles by dodging, yielding, leaping, and lowering, and also the opposite active shapes involved in bows, javelins, and blows. The peaceful dance is then considered, but Bacchic dances and the imitations of drunken Nymphs, Pans, Silenuses, and Satyrs around purifications and initiations are hard to classify as peaceful or warlike."
limits: This records the opening dance taxonomy. It does not include the later rule that the civic dances must be consecrated and left unchanged.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: civic, dance, warlike, peaceful, gods, pleasures, motions, moderation, in tune, tunefulness
observation: Bacchic ritual dance is excluded from civic dance, leaving warlike and peaceful dance as the city's own forms. Peaceful dance honors gods in good fortune and varies by the intensity of pleasure and the dancer's moderation; rightly ordered motion is named tunefulness, while the two noble dance types are pyrrhic and harmonious peaceful dance.
textual_basis: At 815d-816b, the Athenian says Bacchic dance should be placed apart from both warlike and peaceful dance because it is not civic. They should return to the warlike and peaceful forms as indisputably theirs. The peaceful, unwarlike Muse honors gods and children of gods in dances and has one kind arising in the reputation of doing well; it is divided between joy after escaping labors and dangers and gentler pleasure in preserving and increasing prior goods. In such conditions bodily motions are greater with greater pleasures and smaller with lesser ones; the more orderly and trained toward courage move less, while cowards and those untrained in moderation show stronger changes. Imitation of speech through bodily shapes produced dance, and the old name emmeleia rightly names the dances of those doing well and moderate toward pleasures, establishing pyrrhic as warlike and emmeleia as peaceful.
limits: This records the exclusion of Bacchic dance and the naming of the two noble civic dances. It does not include the law-guardian's consecration task.
review_status: accepted
```

From then on he must move nothing connected with dance or song, so that the same city and citizens pass their lives in the same pleasures as far as possible and live well and happily.

english_gloss: fine, choruses, ugly, laughter, comic things, ridiculous things, prudent, slaves, foreigners, comedy
observation: Comic imitation is necessary to recognize the opposite of noble choruses, but virtuous citizens must not perform both opposites. Citizens learn ridiculous things only to avoid doing or saying them from ignorance, while slaves and hired foreigners are assigned the actual comic imitation.
textual_basis: At 816d-817a, the Athenian says the choruses of fine bodies and noble souls have been completed, but the imitations of ugly bodies and thoughts, turned toward laughter in speech, song, dance, and all their representations, must be viewed and known. Without ridiculous things it is impossible to learn their opposites if one is to be prudent, yet one cannot perform both opposites if one is to share even a little in virtue. Therefore citizens must learn these things so as never through ignorance to do or say ridiculous things needlessly, while slaves and hired foreigners should be ordered to imitate them. No seriousness should ever attach to such things, and no free man or woman should be seen learning them; this is set down as the law and account of comedy.
limits: This records the comedy rule. It does not include the address to tragic poets.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: tragedy, poets, constitution, imitation, life, tragedy, drama, law, officials, chorus
observation: The city answers tragic poets by claiming that its constitution is itself the truest tragedy, an imitation of the finest and best life under true law. Tragic poets may not stage rival public speech to children, women, and the crowd unless officials first judge their songs beside the city's and find them the same or better.
textual_basis: At 817b-817d, the Athenian proposes the answer to tragic poets who ask whether they may come into the city and country with their poetry. The city says that it too is a poet of the finest and best tragedy as far as possible, because the whole constitution is an imitation of the finest and best life, which is truly the truest tragedy. The poets are rivals and competitors in the same craft for the finest drama, which only true law can complete. The city will not easily allow them to set up stages in the marketplace, bring in beautiful-voiced actors louder than the lawgivers, and address children, women, and the whole crowd with mostly contrary claims about the same practices. Officials must first judge whether their speeches are suitable for public utterance; if their songs appear the same as or better than the city's, they will receive a chorus, but otherwise not.
limits: This records the admission rule for tragic poets. It does not include the transition to free citizens' remaining studies.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: chorus, learning, slaves, masters, free people, calculations, numbers, measurement, stars, precision
observation: "After choreia rules separate slave and master practices, free citizens have three remaining studies: calculation and number, measurement of length, plane, and depth, and the natural motions of the stars. The many need the necessary parts, not exact mastery; exact study belongs only to a few to be specified later."
textual_basis: "At 817e-818a, the Athenian says the customs arranged by law for all choreia and its learning should stand, separating the things of slaves from those of masters. He then says free people still have three studies: calculations and matters around numbers as one study, measurement of length, surface, and depth as a second, and third, the natural course of the stars' revolutions relative to one another. The many should not work through all these with precision, but only certain few, to be identified near the end. For the multitude, ignorance of the necessary parts is shameful, while exact inquiry into everything is neither easy nor possible."
limits: This records the three-study curriculum and the precision distinction. It does not include the theological necessity argument for these studies.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: god, necessity, studies, divine, god, daemon, hero, even, odd, count, moon, sun
observation: "The necessary parts of mathematics are called divine necessities: no god, daemon, hero, or divine human who seriously cares for humans could lack basic number, counting, even and odd, day-night reckoning, and knowledge of the moon, sun, and other stars' circuits. These studies must be learned in the right order and mixture before proceeding to other noble studies."
textual_basis: At 818b-818d, the Athenian says the necessary part of these studies cannot be discarded and invokes the saying that not even a god fights necessity, clarifying that this applies to divine necessities rather than ordinary human ones. These are the things without doing or learning which no god, daemon, or hero could seriously care for human beings; a human would be far from divine if unable to know one, two, three, even and odd, to count, to reckon night and day, or to understand the revolutions of moon, sun, and the other stars. It would be foolish to think these are unnecessary for someone who will know any of the finest studies. One must first grasp which parts, how many, when, what with what, what separately, and the whole mixture of them, then learn the other studies under their lead.
limits: This records the necessity argument through 818d. It does not include the continuation after the next marker.
review_status: accepted
```

  The corrective lesson is stated: it is not right to say that the Moon, Sun, and other stars wander. Each always goes one circular path, although it appears to be carried along many paths, and ordinary judgment reverses fastest and slowest.
textual_basis: |
  At 822a, Cleinias asks for the wonderful lesson that youths should learn but the older interlocutors do not know. limits: |
  This records the explicit corrective claim at the marker; it does not include the runner comparison that follows.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 829b, the Athenian says each person must train for war not in war but in peacetime. A city with understanding must campaign no less than one day each month, and more if the officials agree, without guarding against winters or heat. The city should bring out men, women, and children whenever officials decide on a public expedition, or by parts at other times, and should always devise noble games with sacrifices so that battles occur in imitation of war.

observation: War-imitating contests distribute victory prizes and marks of excellence, accompanied by public praise and blame across contests and life. The poets of such encomia and blame must be at least fifty and personally honorable doers of noble deeds, with their poems judged by the educator and law-guardians; the same rules apply to women and men.
textual_basis: "At 829c-829e, the Athenian says the mock battles should imitate war as vividly as possible. Victory prizes and excellence prizes must be distributed, and citizens should make encomia and blame of one another according to how each behaves in the contests and in all of life, adorning the one who seems best and blaming the one who does not. Not every poet may compose these things: the poet must first be at least fifty years old and must not merely possess poetry and music without ever having done a noble and conspicuous deed. Those who are themselves good and honored in the city, craftsmen of noble deeds, may have their poems sung even if they are not naturally musical. Their judgment belongs to the educator and the other law-guardians, who grant only them freedom of speech in music. No one may dare to sing an unapproved Muse, even if sweeter than Thamyras or Orpheus, except sacred poems judged and given to the gods and moderate praise or blame of good men. The same rules about campaigns and poetic freedom apply equally to women and men."
limits: This records prizes, praise/blame, poet eligibility, review, and equal application by sex. It does not include the athlete analogy that follows.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The city is compared to athletes preparing for the greatest contest. Just as boxers and pankratiasts practice daily, imitate contest conditions, use substitutes, and even shadowbox when partners are lacking, the legislator should not fear ridicule over mutual military exercises before the real contest for soul, children, property, and the whole city.
textual_basis: "At 830a-830d, the Athenian asks what sort of people the legislator is rearing: athletes for the greatest contests with countless opponents. If one were rearing boxers, pankratiasts, or other competitors, they would not go straight to the contest without daily prior practice. Boxers would imitate what they will use for victory, bind on balls instead of straps to practice blows and evasions, use lifeless images if training partners were lacking, and even shadowbox alone in the absence of partners. The city's fighting force prepares for a greater contest involving life, children, property, and the whole city; the legislator should not fail to legislate exercises with one another because they may seem ridiculous, but should order small daily campaigns without arms and monthly greater and lesser exercises."
limits: This records the athlete analogy and need for preparatory military exercises. It does not include the concrete field exercises and dangerous missiles next.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: Monthly war exercises should move through the whole country, contesting over positions, ambushes, and every warlike imitation, with mock fighting and missiles close enough to reality to create fear. Honors and dishonors distinguish the courageous, and accidental killing in such exercises is cleansed by law rather than treated as ordinary blood-guilt.
textual_basis: "At 830e-831a, the Athenian describes greater and lesser monthly exercises across the whole country: competitors contest for the capture of places, ambushes, and every imitation of warfare. They should use ball-fighting and throws as close as possible to the real thing, with somewhat dangerous missiles, so the game against one another is not wholly fearless but creates fear and reveals the courageous and the non-courageous. By rightly assigning honors to some and dishonors to others, the city is prepared through life for the true contest. If someone dies in this context, the killing is involuntary; after lawful purification, the killer is clean-handed, because the legislator judges that the loss of a few people is less harmful than the death of fear as a test for better and worse people."
limits: This records the realistic drill design, honor distribution, and accidental-death purification rule. It does not include the later explanation of why cities usually lack such training.
review_status: accepted

observation: The absence of such martial choreia and contests in cities is not simply blamed on ignorance. The speaker says there are two sufficient causes, beginning with the desire for wealth, which leaves citizens no leisure for anything except private property and daily gain.
textual_basis: At 831b-831c, Clinias agrees that the whole city should legislate and practice such things, and the Athenian asks whether they know why this kind of choreia and contest exists almost nowhere in cities except in very small traces. He rejects the explanation that this is due to ignorance among the many and among lawgivers. Instead, he says there are two sufficient causes. The first is the lifelong desire for wealth, which makes people without leisure to care for anything except their private possessions; the citizen's whole soul is hung from these, so it can care for nothing except daily profit.
limits: This records the question and the first cause as introduced. It does not include the fuller indictment of money-love that follows.
review_status: accepted

  - τυραννικοὺς
english_gloss: gold, silver, insatiability, rich, pious, impious, merchants, shipowners, robbers, tyrannical
observation: The first cause is an insatiable love of gold and silver that makes cities neglect noble practices, including war training. It bends orderly people into commercial service and bold people into robbery, temple-robbing, warlike crime, and tyranny, leaving them spiritually hungry and unfortunate despite natural ability.
textual_basis: At 831d-832b, the Athenian says the desire for gold and silver makes every man willing to endure every art and device, noble or shameful, if it will make him rich, and to perform pious, impious, or altogether shameful actions if they provide the power to eat, drink, and satisfy sexual appetite in every way. This is one cause preventing cities from adequately practicing any noble thing or the things of war. It makes naturally orderly people into merchants, shipowners, and servants, while it makes the courageous into robbers, burglars, temple-robbers, warlike and tyrannical people, sometimes not without natural gifts but unfortunate, because they must go through life with a hungry soul. Clinias restates that this insatiable search leaves each person without leisure and blocks proper military training.
limits: This records the full wealth-love cause. It does not include the second cause concerning false constitutions.
review_status: accepted
```

Since rulers fear the ruled, they do not willingly allow them to become noble, wealthy, strong, courageous, or warlike; the proposed city escapes both this cause and money-love through leisure, mutual freedom, and anti-wealth laws."
textual_basis: "At 832c-832d, the Athenian identifies the second cause as the so-called constitutions he has often mentioned: democracy, oligarchy, and tyranny. None is a constitution; all are more rightly called faction-regimes, since none rules willing people willingly, but rules willing and unwilling people with continual force. A ruler who fears the ruled will never willingly allow him to become noble, wealthy, strong, courageous, or generally warlike. The city now being discussed has escaped both causes: it has great leisure, citizens are free from one another, and they should become least money-loving from these laws. Therefore this constitution alone could reasonably receive the military education and play just described."
limits: This records the second cause and why the proposed city can receive martial education. It does not include the subsequent gymnastic contest rules.
review_status: accepted

Neither has its greatest use apart from arms. The herald should first call the stadion runner into the contests as now, but the runner enters with arms; they will set no prizes for an unarmed competitor. The first entrant competes in the stadion with arms, the second in the diaulos."

They wait for each group and give victory prizes. The contests are threefold: one for boys, one for beardless youths, and one for men, with the beardless running two-thirds of the adult distance and boys half of that, both archers and hoplites. For females, prepubescent girls race naked in stadion, diaulos, horse-course, and long race, while girls from thirteen until marriage, not after twenty and not before eighteen, compete in fitting dress."

observation: Heavy strength contests are replaced by combat in arms, from one-on-one up to ten-on-ten, with expert rulemaking to define victory and defeat as wrestling experts did. Peltast contests are set against pankration, using bows, shields, javelins, stones, and slings, and the same rules apply to females until marriage.
textual_basis: At 833e-834a, the Athenian turns from races to strength events. Instead of wrestling and other current heavy contests, the contest should be fighting in arms, with one against one, two against two, and up to ten against ten. Just as wrestling experts have legislated what counts as fine and not fine wrestling, the best experts in fighting in arms should be called to legislate who is justly victor in such battles, by what he has done or avoided suffering, and likewise what distinguishes the defeated. The same should be legislated for females until marriage. Whole peltast fighting should be set against pankration, with competitors using bows, shields, javelins, hand-thrown stones, and slings, and prizes and victories distributed to those who best render the legal requirements.
limits: This records the armed combat and peltast contest rules. It does not include horse contests.
review_status: accepted

observation: "Horse contests are adapted to Crete's limited use for horses: no chariot ambitions, but single-horse contests by age class and armed dismounting judged by tribal and cavalry officers. Unarmed contests are excluded, while mounted archery and javelin contests remain useful; female participation is not forced by law but may be allowed if prior training makes it natural."
textual_basis: At 834b-834d, the Athenian says horse contests follow next, but Crete has neither many horses nor great need of them, so zeal for breeding and contests must be less. There is no chariot-rearer and no reasonable ambition for chariots, so to set chariot contestants would show no sense. By setting prizes for single horses, foals, intermediate horses, and full-grown horses, they give horsemanship play according to the nature of the country. The law gives common judgment of all these races and armed dismounting contests to tribe-commanders and cavalry-commanders. It would not be right to establish unarmed contests either in gymnastic events or here. A Cretan mounted archer or javelin-thrower is not useless, so there should be rivalry and contest for these as play. For females, the law should not force participation by commands, but if earlier education has become habit and nature permits girls or maidens to share without distress, they should be allowed and not blamed.
limits: This records the horse-contest adaptation. It does not include the conclusion of gymnastic and musical contest legislation.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 834e-835b, the Athenian says contest and learning in gymnastics, both in competitions and daily work under teachers, now have their end, and most of music has likewise been completed. The remaining matters of rhapsodes and their followers, and necessary festival competitions of choruses, will be arranged when months, days, and years are assigned to the gods and those with gods, whether in three-year periods, five-year periods, or however the gods give understanding about order. Musical contests should then be expected to be contested in parts, arranged by prize-managers, the educator of the young, and the law-guardians, who come together and become lawmakers concerning when, who, and with whom contests around all choruses and choreia will occur. The first legislator has often said what each should be in speech, songs, harmonies, rhythms, and dances, and secondary lawmakers must follow these models and assign contests fittingly to each sacrifice at proper times, giving the city festivals to celebrate.

textual_basis: At 835c, the Athenian says some ordering details are not hard to understand and would not bring great gain or loss if moved here or there. But the matters that make no small difference are hard to persuade about and would most of all be a god's work, if commands could come from him. In the present situation they seem to need a bold human being who especially honors frank speech, says what seems best for city and citizens, sets in corrupted souls what is fitting and consequent on the whole constitution, speaks against the greatest desires, and has no human helper, following reason alone by himself.

textual_basis: "At 836d-836e, the Athenian says this case does not agree with what they always say the lawgiver must watch. He asks what part toward virtue would be contributed if the current practice were allowed to be legislated as noble or not at all shameful: whether the character of courage would be implanted in the soul of the persuaded, or the kind belonging to a moderate form in the persuader. He then says no one would ever be persuaded of these claims; rather everyone would blame softness in the one who yields to pleasures and cannot endure, and would also blame the likeness of the image in the one going toward imitation of the female."

  - τέχνην
  - θέσεως
english_gloss: body, soul, desire, outrage, moderate, courageous, magnificent, prudent, keep pure, virtue, law, prevent, agreement, art, placement
observation: The span contrasts a body-focused lover, who urges satiety and gives no honor to the beloved's soul-character, with a soul-focused lover, who treats bodily fullness as outrage and wants reciprocal purity. After naming a mixed third love, the discussion asks whether law should block all loves or admit the virtue-oriented one that wants the young person to become best while blocking the other two if possible. It then marks the placement of this law as partly easy and partly very hard.
textual_basis: At 837c-838a, the Athenian contrasts a lover of body and season, hungry as for fruit, with one who treats bodily desire as secondary and desires soul by soul, respecting moderation, courage, magnificence, and prudence, and wanting purity with a pure beloved. He names a third love mixed from both, then asks whether law must prevent all loves, or whether the city should contain the virtue love that wants the young person to become best and should prevent the other two if possible. Megillus accepts the statement; the Athenian takes his agreement, postpones persuading Clinias, and says the art of setting this law is currently in one way easy and in another as hard as possible.
limits: This records the contrast among loves and the law's initial admit-or-block question within the span. It does not use the prior definition of friendship or the unwritten-law example that follows.
review_status: accepted
```

The reason given is that each person hears this said from birth, always and everywhere, in comic contexts and in serious tragedy, including named mythical examples where offenders are shown ready to impose death on themselves as penalty. Megillus says report has remarkable power when no one tries to breathe otherwise against the law. The Athenian concludes that a lawgiver who wants to subdue a desire can know the method: consecrate this report the same way among slaves, free people, children, women, and the whole city, making the strongest settlement for the law."

It is easy to understand how it is possible, because a sufficiently consecrated custom will master every soul and make it obey the established laws through fear. But the matter has advanced so far that it does not seem possible even then, just as the practice of common meals is disbelieved as impossible for a whole city throughout life, even though it has been tested in deed among Clinias' people; the case concerning women still does not seem naturally possible even in those cities. Because of the strength of disbelief, he calls both matters very hard to keep by law.

The same report is attached to Crison, Astylus, Diopompus, and many others. The span also says these athletes were much worse educated in soul than the proposed citizens, while their bodies were much more vigorous, and Clinias confirms that ancient reports said these events actually happened.

He says one should prefer moving any great stone rather than a small boundary stone that marks sworn friendship and enmity before the gods. Zeus is witness in both domestic and foreign forms, and the violator is liable to two judgments, first from the gods and second under law. Anyone may report the mover to the farmers, who bring the case to court, where the court assesses what the convicted party must suffer or pay."

english_gloss: planting, lawmakers, waters, farmers, streams, springs, shrines, tombs, draw water, country-wardens
observation: The legislator declines to restate every small planting rule and instead relies on adequate laws by earlier lawmakers. Water law allows a person to bring water from common streams without cutting private springs, routing it anywhere except through houses, shrines, or tombs, and permits rationed neighbor access when one's own land lacks necessary water.
textual_basis: "At 843e-844b, the Athenian says planting must leave the measure from neighboring lands, as already sufficiently stated by many lawmakers, whose laws should be used rather than forcing the city-ordering legislator to legislate every small matter. He then says old and fine water laws for farmers should not be diverted by speech: whoever wishes to bring water to his land may begin from common streams, without cutting any visible private spring, and may route it where he wishes except through houses, shrines, or tombs, doing no damage beyond the watercourse itself. If natural dryness prevents necessary drinking water, the owner may dig to clay in his own land; failing water there, he may draw from neighbors up to necessary drinking needs, or, when neighbors are also constrained, receive a daily water schedule from the agronomoi."
limits: This records planting-distance deference and basic water access. It does not include rainwater runoff disputes or fruit laws.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: "Rainwater runoff disputes are handled by the appropriate local official: city-warden in town and country-warden in the countryside. Either blocking outflow from above or releasing streams carelessly downward can be regulated, and disobedience to the official order brings double compensation for the harm."
textual_basis: "At 844c-844d, the Athenian describes harms involving waters from Zeus: someone farming or living above may harm those below by denying outflow, while the person above may also harm the lower neighbor by releasing streams at random. If they will not cooperate, anyone may summon an astynomos in the city or an agronomos in the country to order what each must do. The person who does not remain within the order is treated as acting from envy and a difficult soul and, if convicted, pays double the harm to the injured party for refusing to obey the officials."
limits: This records runoff adjudication and penalty. It does not include the fruit-sharing law introduced next.

english_gloss: seasonal fruit, goddess, Dionysian, grapes, figs, Arcturus, Dionysus, bunch of grapes, slave, resident alien
observation: Fruit law distinguishes a playful Dionysian gift from fruit naturally suited for storage. Premature tasting of rustic grapes or figs before the harvest season triggers scaled sacred fines, while noble grapes and figs are freely usable from one's own land but require consent on another's land; slaves are punished by lashes, resident aliens may purchase, and passing strangers may receive limited hospitality.
textual_basis: "At 844d-845b, the Athenian says everyone must share seasonal fruit in a certain way, because the goddess has two gifts: a Dionysian playful one not to be stored, and another naturally made for storage. Anyone who tastes rustic grapes or figs before the time of vintage with Arcturus owes fifty sacred drachmas to Dionysus if from his own land, a mina if from neighbors, and two-thirds of a mina if from others. Noble grapes and noble figs may be enjoyed from one's own land whenever and however one wishes, but taking them from another without persuasion is punished under the rule against moving what one did not lay down. A slave who touches them without the owner's consent is lashed once for each grape or fig. A resident alien may harvest noble fruit by purchase, and a visiting stranger who wants to eat while traveling may touch the noble fruit with one attendant without price as a guest."
limits: This records rules for grapes, figs, slaves, resident aliens, and passing strangers. It does not include the later rule for pears, apples, pomegranates, and similar fruits.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: guest-gifts, rustic, slave, free person, pears, apples, pomegranates, thirty, foreigner, virtue
observation: Rules for ordinary fruits distinguish slaves, free persons, foreigners, younger people, and older citizens. Rustic fruit is barred to foreign guest-sharing, while pears, apples, pomegranates, and similar fruit may be taken secretly without shame; a caught person under thirty may be struck without legal claim, foreigners may share, and older citizens may eat on the spot but risk reputational consequences if they disregard the law.
textual_basis: At 845b-845d, the Athenian excludes foreigners from sharing rustic fruit and similar produce; an ignorant slave who touches it is punished with blows, while an ignorant free person is sent away after instruction to touch other fruit not fit for raisins, wine, or dried figs. Concerning pears, apples, pomegranates, and all such fruit, taking secretly is not shameful, but someone caught under thirty may be beaten without wounds and without any legal action by a free person for those blows. A foreigner may share in such things as with seasonal fruit. If an older man touches them, eating on the spot and carrying nothing away, he shares like the foreigner, but if he does not obey the law he risks being without contest concerning virtue if later judges are reminded of such conduct.
limits: This records ordinary fruit access by status and age. It does not include deliberate water corruption.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: Because garden water is especially nourishing and uniquely easy to corrupt, deliberate harm to another's water by poisoning, digging, or theft is litigated before the city-wardens. A convicted poisoner must pay the assessed harm and purify the springs or water vessel according to interpreter rules.
textual_basis: At 845d-845e, the Athenian says water is exceptionally nourishing for gardens but easily corrupted, unlike earth, sun, and winds. Poisonings, diversions, and thefts are all possible with water, so a helping law is needed. If anyone deliberately corrupts another's water, whether spring-water or collected water, by poisonings, diggings, or thefts, the injured person brings suit before the astynomoi and registers the value of the damage. If the convicted person has harmed by poisonings, he must, in addition to the assessed value, purify the springs or water vessel in the way the interpreter laws prescribe for each case.
limits: This records deliberate water corruption and remedy. It does not include the harvest transport rule beginning after this span.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: Many small procedural rules are necessary but not worthy of the old lawgiver's direct legislation. Younger lawmakers are to imitate prior legislation, set small rules beside great ones from practical experience until the system seems adequate, and then make them fixed for use in life.
textual_basis: At 846b-846c, the Athenian says there are countless small legal rules according to which penalties must occur, including deadlines for suits, summonses, summoners, whether two or more must be called, and similar matters. These cannot be left unlegislated, yet they are not worthy of an old lawgiver. He says the young should legislate them by imitating the prior laws, setting small rules beside great ones, and holding experience of their necessary use until all seems adequately established. At that point they make them unmoved and use them as a measure while living.
limits: This records delegation of minor procedural lawmaking. It does not include the craft laws beginning after this procedural aside.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: craftsmen, native, household slave, craft, citizen, city, order, smithing, carpentry, virtue
observation: "No native citizen or citizen's household slave is to labor at craft trades, because the citizen already possesses the demanding craft of preserving and acquiring the city's common order. The law also enforces one person, one craft: smithing and carpentry may not be combined, nor may someone supervise another craft as a profit-making pretext."
textual_basis: At 846d-847b, the Athenian says no native should be among those who labor around craftwork, nor any household slave of a native man. A citizen has a sufficient craft, requiring much practice and many studies, in preserving and acquiring the common order of the city, and this is not something to pursue as a side task. He adds that almost no human nature can practice two pursuits or crafts accurately, or practice one while supervising another. Therefore no smith should at the same time be a carpenter, and no carpenter should supervise smiths rather than his own craft on the pretext that many household slaves create more income for him. Each person in the city is to possess one craft and gain a living from it. The city-wardens preserve this law; a native turning toward a craft more than care for virtue is corrected by reproaches and dishonors, while a foreigner practicing two crafts is punished by bonds, money penalties, and expulsion until compelled to be one and not many.
limits: This records exclusion of citizens from crafts and the one-craft rule. It does not include import-export controls.
review_status: accepted
```

The twelve law-guardians after the five eldest are removed are made recognizers and supervisors of these matters.

english_gloss: food, distribution, Cretan, law, twelve, wheat, barley, free persons, household slaves, foreigners
observation: "Food distribution is modeled near Cretan law: all produce is divided into twelve parts according to consumption, and each twelfth is divided into three proportional shares. One share is for free persons, one for their household slaves, and one for craftsmen, resident foreigners, and visitors needing necessities; only the third share must be saleable."
textual_basis: "At 847e-848b, the Athenian turns to food and distribution of what comes from the land and says an arrangement near the correctness of Cretan law seems fitting. Everyone must divide all that comes from the land into twelve parts according to how it is to be consumed. Each twelfth part, such as wheat and barley and all other seasonal produce following them, together with all animals saleable in each part, is divided three ways according to ratio: one part for free persons, one for their household slaves, and the third for craftsmen and all foreigners, including resident aliens needing necessary food and those arriving for some public or private need. This third share alone is necessarily saleable, while nothing from the two other shares must be sold."
limits: This records the twelvefold and threefold distribution rule. It does not include village settlement and market oversight.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 848c-848e, the Athenian turns from distribution to dwellings and says twelve villages should be set out, each at the center of a twelfth part. In each village, shrines and a market are first reserved for gods and attendant daemons, old local foundations are honored, and shrines for Hestia, Zeus, Athena, and each part's founder are established. Buildings are first placed around these shrines where the site is highest for secure guard reception, and the remaining land is arranged by dividing craftsmen into thirteen parts, settling one in the city and suitable kinds in each village. The agronomoi oversee how many and what sorts each place needs and where they will live with least trouble and most benefit to farmers.

limits: This record does not include the Athenian's answer, which only begins within the resolved span and is not complete here.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 858a-858c, the Athenian says their present good fortune is that there is no necessity to legislate; they can examine every constitution and try to see both the best and the most necessary way it might come to be, choosing which to inspect. Clinias calls the proposed choice ridiculous, since they are not like lawgivers forced by great necessity to legislate immediately with no tomorrow. With divine permission, they may act like stone-gatherers or beginners of another construction, bringing materials in bulk from which fitting parts will be selected for the future construction at leisure. He proposes that they are not compulsory builders but those still setting some materials beside them and arranging others, so it is right to speak of some laws as set and others as merely laid beside.
limits: This records the leisure-and-materials model for law inquiry. It does not include the discussion of written law as civic writing.

textual_basis: "At 860d-860e, the Athenian asks how their own account stands with consistency and restates that all bad people are altogether bad unwillingly. Thus the wrongdoer would appear to do wrong unwillingly to someone who posits injustice as involuntary, and the Athenian says he agrees that all do wrong unwillingly, despite possible claims that some are unwillingly unjust but willingly do wrong from love of victory or honor. He then frames the question of Magnesian legislation: whether to legislate at all, and whether to define voluntary and involuntary injustices with larger penalties for voluntary cases and smaller ones for involuntary cases, or equal penalties because no injustices are voluntary at all."

english_gloss: injustices, voluntary, involuntary, just things, disturbance, discord, is legislated, defining, lawful, holy
observation: The Athenian says the claim that all injustice is involuntary cannot simply replace ordinary legal distinctions. Before assigning penalties, they must show that there are two relevant kinds and define their difference; otherwise no one can judge whether a penalty has been fittingly set. He refuses to suppress the involuntary-injustice thesis, but says the two kinds must differ by something other than voluntary and involuntary in the usual way.
textual_basis: At 861a-861d, Clinias asks how to use the present claims. The Athenian recalls that they had just said there is much disturbance and discord about just things, and asks whether, without finding a way through and defining how these differ, they can legislate as though all lawgivers everywhere correctly posit two kinds of injustices, voluntary and involuntary. He rejects merely uttering a godlike thesis without explanation and says it is necessary before legislation to make clear that the two kinds exist and that their difference is otherwise, so that when a penalty is attached to either kind everyone can follow and judge the fittingness of the enactment. Clinias says they must either stop saying all injustices are involuntary or first define why that claim is correct. The Athenian refuses not to say what he thinks true, since that would not be lawful or holy, and says they must try to show the two kinds by some other difference.
limits: This records the methodological demand for definition before penalty law. It does not include the harm-versus-injustice distinction introduced next.
review_status: accepted
```
