english_gloss: harms, associations, voluntary, involuntary, injustices, benefit, character, manner, laws, friendship
observation: "The Athenian distinguishes harms from injustices: voluntary and involuntary elements abound in civic interactions, but not every harm is an injustice. Unwilled harm is not to be legislated as involuntary injustice, while wrongly produced benefit can still be unjust; the legislator must look both to injustice and to harm, restoring damaged things where possible and using compensation to move doers and sufferers from conflict toward friendship."
textual_basis: At 861e-862c, the Athenian says many harms arise among citizens in associations and dealings, and voluntary and involuntary elements are abundant in them. He warns against treating all harms as injustices and then dividing injustices into voluntary and involuntary, since involuntary harms are not fewer than voluntary harms in number or magnitude. He says he will not call it injustice when someone harms another unwillingly and not wanting to do so, and will not legislate that as an involuntary injustice, whether the harm is larger or smaller. Conversely, if his account prevails, a person can do injustice by being the cause of a benefit that is not rightly produced. Giving or taking away something should not simply be called just or unjust; the legislator must look to whether someone benefits or harms another by using character and a just manner, and must look to both injustice and harm. The harmed thing should be made sound by laws as far as possible, saving what is lost, setting upright what is fallen, making sound what is killed or wounded, and after compensation for each harm, trying always to establish doers and sufferers from difference into friendship.
limits: This records the distinction between harm and injustice and the restorative aim of law. It does not include the next claim about curing unjust harms as diseases in the soul.
review_status: accepted
```

They may use deeds, speeches, pleasures, pains, honors, dishonors, money penalties, gifts, or any means that makes a person hate injustice and accept the just; when the lawgiver sees an incurable condition, death is assigned because such persons do not benefit by living and others benefit from their removal.

He lists possible means: deeds, speeches, pleasures, pains, honors, dishonors, money penalties, gifts, and any way that makes someone hate injustice and love or not hate the nature of the just. This is the work of the finest laws. For those the lawgiver perceives as incurable in these matters, he says they neither live better themselves nor benefit others except by departing life, becoming an example not to commit injustice and making the city empty of bad men; for such errors the lawgiver must assign death."

observation: The clarification of injustice begins from three psychic sources of error. Spirit is a difficult, combative possession that overturns many things by irrational force; pleasure is a different power that rules by persuasion with deception; ignorance is a third cause, and lawgiving should divide simple ignorance from double ignorance that combines not knowing with a conceit of wisdom.
textual_basis: "At 863b-863e, the Athenian says they already hear and say that in the soul there is spirit, whether passion or part, naturally implanted as a contentious and hard-fighting possession that overturns many things by irrational force. He distinguishes pleasure from spirit and says pleasure rules from an opposite power by persuasion with deception, doing whatever its wish wants. He then names ignorance as a third cause of errors. A better lawgiver divides it in two: simple ignorance is the cause of light errors, while double ignorance occurs when someone is held not only by ignorance but by the opinion of wisdom, as if he knew completely what he does not know at all. With strength and force this causes great and unmusical errors; with weakness it causes errors of children and elders, for which the laws should be gentlest and most full of pardon."
limits: This records the tripartite source account and the twofold ignorance distinction. It does not include the following formal definition of injustice.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: "For penalty law, the three disclosed sources of error are recalled and subdivided into five kinds: pain, called spirit and fear; pleasure and desires; and pursuit by hopes and true opinion about the best, with the latter itself split. These five kinds require different laws and fall into two modes: open violent acts and hidden acts with darkness and deception, with some cases combining both and requiring the harshest laws if proportionate."
textual_basis: At 864a-864c, the Athenian says that since three kinds of errors have been disclosed, they should be recalled more firmly. One kind is pain, which they call spirit and fear; a second is pleasure and desires; a third is the pursuit of hopes and true opinion concerning the best. When this third itself is split, the three become five kinds, and laws differing from one another must be set for the five kinds in two classes. The classes are actions done through violent and manifest acts, and acts done secretly with darkness and deception; sometimes a deed is done through both, and in such cases laws would be harshest if they had their fitting share.
limits: This records the classification schema up to 864c. It does not include the return to individual high-crime laws beginning after this span.

observation: The law distinguishes major public crimes committed in a diminished condition from ordinary liability. When madness, disease, extreme old age, or childish play is made evident to selected judges, the actor pays simple damage and is released from other legal penalties, except that a homicide impurity still requires absence from the country.
textual_basis: At 864d-864e, the speaker lists temple plunder, betrayal, and corruption of the laws toward dissolving the constitution, then introduces cases where the actor is mad, constrained by disease or extreme old age, or acting like a child. If the selected judges find that the transgression was done in this condition, the text requires simple repayment of damage, releases other penalties, but requires a killer to live abroad for a year and imposes two years of public imprisonment if he returns early or enters his own country.
limits: This record only covers the diminished-condition rule and its immediate homicide exception. It does not cover the later involuntary-homicide categories.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: A parent-killer acting from anger receives different treatment depending on release by the dying parent. Release lets the killer follow the involuntary-homicide purification pattern and become clean; without release, the act is placed under assault, impiety, and sacrilege, and death is prescribed because the law will not permit even lethal self-defense against parents.
textual_basis: At 869a-869c, the speaker describes someone uncontrolled by anger toward parents. If the dying parent willingly releases the killer before death, the killer is purified like those who committed involuntary homicide and becomes clean. If there is no release, the killer is liable to the severest assault suits, impiety, and sacrilege, and the span argues that no law grants permission to kill father or mother even when one is about to die at parental hands, ending with death as the penalty for killing father or mother in anger.
limits: This record covers the anger case against parents. It does not cover premeditated parental murder or the later self-defense rules for non-parental cases.
review_status: accepted

english_gloss: factions, fight, defending, enemy, clean, citizen, foreigner, slave, free person, release, exile abroad
observation: Defensive homicide is sorted by status relation. A brother, citizen, foreigner, or slave who kills an equal-status first aggressor in a fight is clean, and citizen-foreigner pairs receive the same clean status. A slave who kills a free person while defending himself is instead liable under the same laws as a parent-killer. Voluntary release by the victim makes these cases follow involuntary-homicide purification with one year abroad.
textual_basis: At 869c-869e, the speaker says a brother who kills a brother during factional fighting while defending against one who began violence is clean as if killing an enemy, and extends the same rule to citizen against citizen, foreigner against foreigner, citizen against foreigner, foreigner against citizen, and slave against slave. The same span then makes a slave who kills a free person in self-defense liable under the parent-killer laws, and generalizes release so that if any victim willingly releases any such killer as having committed involuntary homicide, purifications occur and the legal exile is one year.
limits: This record covers self-defense and release mechanics in this span. It does not claim that all defensive killings in the dialogue are treated alike.
review_status: rejected

english_gloss: desire, soul, longings, money, acquisition, lack of education, wealth, body, soul, justly, moderately
observation: The prelude names uncontrolled desire in a soul made savage by longings as the greatest source of voluntary murder, especially desire for unlimited acquisition of money. The corrective argument ranks wealth below goods of body and soul and says the happy person should seek to be wealthy justly and moderately, not simply seek wealth.
textual_basis: At 870a-870c, the speaker begins the account of voluntary and unjust killings by naming the greatest cause as desire ruling a soul made savage by longings. The strongest instance is the power connected with money and unlimited acquisition, which is tied to bad education and bad praise of wealth. The same span says wealth is third because it is for the body's sake and the body is for the soul's sake, then states that the person who will be happy should not seek to be rich, but to be rich justly and moderately.
limits: This record covers the wealth-desire cause and its corrective ranking. It does not cover the later ambition, envy, fear, and written-law procedure.
review_status: accepted

observation: For intentional and unjust kin homicide by one's own hand, the law first bars the killer from lawful civic and sacred spaces so that those places are not polluted. Relatives within the cousinship on both male and female sides who fail to prosecute or proclaim the exclusion take pollution and divine enmity upon themselves and become liable to anyone willing to punish on behalf of the dead. The avenger must complete the required lustrations and proclamations before compelling trial.
textual_basis: At 871a-871c, the written law concerns someone who intentionally and unjustly kills any kin member by his own hand. The killer is first excluded from sacred places, marketplace, harbors, and every common assembly, whether or not any person announces this to him, because the law announces it for the whole city. The same span says a relative within cousinship who fails to prosecute when required, or fails to proclaim exclusion, receives the pollution and divine enmity and becomes liable to anyone willing to punish for the dead. It then requires the willing avenger to complete the relevant lustration guard and other divine customs, make the proclamation, and compel the killer to undergo trial according to law.
limits: This record covers pretrial exclusion, kin enforcement, and avenger preparation. It does not include the later judge selection, conviction penalty, or fugitive rule.
review_status: accepted

observation: The homicide procedure leaves divine-facing details to institutional specification. The lawgiver can say that prayers and sacrifices to the relevant gods are needed to prevent murders in cities, but the guardians of the laws, interpreters, seers, and the god are to legislate the correct divine mode for introducing these suits. The judges are the same as for temple-robbery cases; conviction brings death and no burial in the victim's land, while flight from trial becomes permanent exile.
textual_basis: At 871c-871d, the speaker says it is easy for the lawgiver to declare that such matters must occur through prayers and sacrifices to gods concerned with preventing murders in cities. The same span assigns the more exact divine procedure for introducing these suits to guardians of the laws acting with interpreters, seers, and the god. It then names the judges as the same ones appointed for sacred-plunder cases, assigns death and denial of burial in the victim's land to the convicted person, and assigns perpetual exile to the one who flees and refuses trial.
limits: This record covers the procedural delegation and penalties within 871c-871d. It does not continue into the next marker's rule about what happens if the fugitive enters the victim's territory.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The slave homicide rule distinguishes two cases. A slave who willingly kills a free person, whether directly or by counsel, is taken by the city's public executioner toward the victim's tomb, flogged as the successful prosecutor orders, and killed if still alive. A person who kills a slave who has done no wrong, from fear that the slave may disclose shameful and bad deeds or for a similar reason, is to undergo homicide suits just as if he had killed a citizen.
textual_basis: At 872b-872c, the text first keeps the direct-handed and plotted-homicide distinction for slaves, then states that a slave convicted of willingly killing a free person is brought near the dead person's tomb, flogged at the successful prosecutor's command, and put to death if he survives the blows. It then adds that killing a slave who has done no wrong, because he might become an informer of shameful and bad acts or for a like reason, is subject to the same homicide suits as killing a citizen.
limits: This records slave-related homicide penalties and lawsuit equivalence for an innocent slave victim. It does not cover the following kin-killing prelude.
review_status: accepted

For conviction in this kind of homicide, court servants and officials kill the offender, cast the body naked at a fixed crossroads outside the city, and every official casts a stone on the corpse's head on behalf of the whole city, purifying the city as a whole. After that, they carry the corpse to the borders of the country and cast it out unburied according to law.
limits: This records the civic penalty for intentional kin homicide. It does not include the separate treatment of self-killing that begins after this penalty.

The remaining ritual matters are said to be known by the god, so the nearest kin are to ask interpreters and follow the laws for purifications and burials. The graves for such persons are to be alone, with no co-burial, placed among unused and unnamed parts of the twelve border regions, and not marked by stele or name.
limits: This records the specified self-killing case and its burial restrictions. It does not cover animal, object, or unknown-killer homicide rules.

english_gloss: beasts, nature, advantageous things, civic order, political, art, private, common, greed, private action, pleasure
observation: "The need for law is explained by a defect in ordinary human nature: people are not reliably sufficient to know what benefits civic life and, after knowing, to choose and do the best. True political art must care for the common rather than the private, because the common binds cities while private interest tears them apart; mortal nature turns even an unaccountable ruler toward gain, private action, avoidance of pain, and pursuit of pleasure."
textual_basis: "At 875a-875b, the Athenian says humans must set laws and live by laws or differ little from the wildest beasts. He gives the reason: human nature is not sufficient to know what benefits humans for civic order and, after knowing, always to be able and willing to do the best. He says true political art must care for the common, not the private, since the common binds cities and the private separates them, and that mortal nature turns an unaccountable and self-ruling civic ruler toward greed and private action while fleeing pain and pursuing pleasure."
limits: This records the political-anthropological reason for law. It does not include the following rare divine exception or the second-best account of law and order.
review_status: accepted
```

Because such a condition is nowhere available except in small measure, law and order are chosen as the second-best framework, especially for assigning what a person who wounds or harms another must suffer or pay.

He immediately adds that this is not present anywhere except slightly, so the second option must be chosen: order and law, which see and look to the general case but cannot cover every case. He then turns this point toward the problem of what a wounder or harmer must suffer or pay."
limits: This records the second-best status of law and its application to injury penalties. It does not include the later account of good and bad courts.

english_gloss: courts, base, judgments, noise, penalties, to legislate, having been educated, having been tested, judges, outlines
observation: The amount of penalty discretion delegated to courts depends on the quality of the courts. Base, secretive, noisy courts should receive only the smallest discretion while the lawgiver states most penalties directly; well-established courts with educated and tested judges may judge many matters about what offenders should suffer or pay. For the present law code, the Athenian proposes giving judges the greatest and largest matters while still supplying outlines, types, and examples so judgment does not step outside justice.
textual_basis: At 876b-876e, the Athenian contrasts defective courts that conceal opinions or judge noisily like theaters with courts correctly established as far as possible, whose future judges have been well educated and carefully tested. In the first kind of city, he says only the smallest penalty decisions should be entrusted to courts while the lawgiver states most matters explicitly. In the better case, it is proper to entrust many decisions about what offenders should suffer or pay. He then says their present judges can receive the greatest and most numerous matters, provided the lawgiver gives outlines, types, and examples of penalties so they never go outside justice.
limits: This records the court-discretion rule and its safeguards. It does not give the later specific wound penalties that follow after the return to the laws.
review_status: accepted
```

It then states the law for striking someone twenty or more years older: suitable bystanders must separate the fighters or defend the older injured party as a brother, father, or still higher relation; the offender faces an assault case and at least one year bound if convicted. Foreigners and metics receive the same bystander-aid rule but two-year and three-year binding terms respectively, unless the court values a longer penalty."
limits: This records the equal-age fighting rule, the elder-assault intervention rule, and the status-scaled detention penalties. It does not include the separate explanatory prelude about laws for good and bad characters.

greek_terms:
  - δοῦλος
  - ἐλεύθερον

  - συνδήσαντες

english_gloss: slave, free person, foreigner, citizen, let him help, binding together, fetters, having whipped, master, owner, women
observation: If a slave strikes a free person, whether foreigner or citizen, a bystander must help or pay the stated status-based fine. Bystanders bind the slave together with the person struck and hand him to the injured party; that person may fetter and whip him as much as desired without damaging the master, then return him to the owner. The owner may not release the bound slave until the slave persuades the injured person that he deserves to live released; the same legal rules apply for women with women, women with men, and men with women.
textual_basis: At 882a-882c, the law says that when a slave strikes a free person, whether foreigner or citizen, the bystander must help or pay the stated fine. Those present bind the slave with the person struck and deliver him to the injured party, who binds him in fetters, whips him as many times as desired without harming the master, and gives him back to the owner. The owner who receives him bound must not release him until the slave persuades the struck person that he is worthy to live unbound; the text then extends the same rules across female-female and female-male cases.
limits: This records the slave-on-free assault procedure and its gender extension. It does not include the prior parent-assault pollution rule that overlaps the opening of 882a.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The Athenian identifies the arguments of newer wise figures as a source of impiety because they answer divine-evidence appeals by recasting sun, moon, stars, and earth as earth and stones unable to care for human affairs.
textual_basis: At 886d-886e, the Athenian sets aside the ancient accounts and says the newer wise figures should be blamed where they are causes of bad things. He says their arguments work by taking the very things offered as proofs that gods exist, including sun, moon, stars, and earth as gods and divine things, and persuading hearers to call them earth and stones unable to care for human affairs, with these arguments wrapped persuasively.
limits: This records the text's stated account of a rival teaching. It does not include the preceding assessment of ancient theogonic accounts or independently identify any historical school.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 890e-891a Clinias compares the willingness to hear long discussions of drinking and music with the need to endure long useful arguments about gods, then identifies written stability as a legislative help.
limits: The record covers the reason given for written long argument and does not summarize the whole theology to be defended.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The Athenian identifies a source of impious natural inquiry in the claim that fire, water, earth, and air are first among all things and are what nature names, while soul comes later from them. He treats this as a root of unintelligent opinion among those who handle natural investigations badly.
textual_basis: At 891c-891d, the Athenian says the speaker of the opposed doctrine regards fire, water, earth, and air as first among all things, calls these nature, and makes soul later from them. He then asks whether they have discovered a kind of source of unintelligent opinion among people who ever took up inquiries about nature, warning that it matters if impious speakers misuse arguments and lead others.
limits: This records the diagnosis of the opposed naturalist ordering. It does not yet include the positive claim that soul is prior to body.

english_gloss: generation, destruction, cause, soul, among first, bodies, change, intellect, art, law, nature
observation: "The counterargument says the impious accounts invert priority: what is first cause of generation and destruction is made later, and what is later is made prior. Soul must be understood as among the first things, older than bodies, and ruling their changes; therefore opinion, care, intellect, art, and law are prior to bodily qualities, and if soul is first, nature is more properly said of soul than of fire or air."
textual_basis: "At 891e-892c, the Athenian says the speeches forming impious souls have made the first cause of generation and destruction later, and the later thing prior, causing error about the being of gods. He explains that almost everyone is ignorant of soul, especially its generation and power: soul is among the first things, comes before all bodies, and especially rules all their change and reordering. From this he says things kindred to soul, including opinion, care, intellect, art, and law, would be prior to hard, soft, heavy, and light. He adds that if soul is shown to be prior, then nature is most correctly said of soul rather than fire or air."
limits: This records the priority argument up to the announced need to prove soul older than body. It does not include the later motion proof itself.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 892d-893a, the Athenian warns them to guard against a deceptive argument that might mislead them as elders and make them ridiculous. He introduces the image of three people crossing a strong river, with himself as the youngest and experienced in currents, testing first while leaving the others safe. Applying the analogy, he says the coming argument may be stronger and nearly impassable for their strength, so he should question himself first, answer himself again, and carry the whole argument through until it completes the account of soul and shows soul before body.
limits: This records the procedural method and river analogy. It does not include the actual first questions of the proof.
review_status: accepted
```

He extends the same account to stars, moon, years, months, and seasons: since soul or souls have appeared as their causes and are good with every virtue, they should be called gods, whether they order the whole heaven in bodies or in some other way."
textual_basis: At 899a-899b, the argument moves from the sun's guiding soul to the general celestial case. The cause of the sun's light is to be regarded as divine, and the same reasoning is applied to all stars, the moon, years, months, and seasons.
limits: This records the conclusion that good celestial souls are gods. It does not include the closing terms later set for the person who still denies gods.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 904e-905b, the speech says that worse souls go toward worse souls and better souls toward better ones, in life and in deaths, and that neither the addressee nor any unlucky person can outrun this divine justice. limits: This records the warning about inescapable divine justice and apparent impious success. It does not include the following transition to the separate claim about gods accepting gifts.

He then describes beastlike unjust souls trying to persuade guardian souls by flatteries and prayerlike charms, and identifies greed as disease in bodies, plague in seasons, and injustice in cities and regimes.

observation: The claim that unjust people can buy divine forgiveness is made to look absurd by guardian analogies. It would be like wolves giving dogs a little of their plunder so that the dogs allow the flock to be ravaged, or like pilots, charioteers, commanders, physicians, farmers, herdsmen, or dogs betraying their task because of offerings or gifts.
textual_basis: "At 906d-907a, the Athenian formulates the claim that gods are always forgiving toward unjust people if they receive a share from injustices, comparing it to wolves giving dogs a small portion of plunder so that the dogs allow flocks to be seized. He then asks which earlier guardian analogy could fit gods without making the speaker ridiculous: pilots turned aside by libation and savor while wrecking ships, charioteers bribed to betray victory, commanders, physicians, farmers, herdsmen, or dogs charmed by wolves."
limits: This records the analogy-based refutation of divine bribability. It does not include the concluding claim that this opinion is the worst form of impiety.
review_status: accepted
```

The three proposed claims are then declared adequately proved: gods exist, gods care, and gods are wholly unappeasable against justice."
textual_basis: "At 907a-907b, the Athenian asks whether all the gods, the greatest guardians over the greatest things and superior in guardianship by virtue, could be called worse than dogs and average humans who would never betray justice for gifts from unjust men. Clinias says no and calls the view the worst and most impious. The Athenian then asks whether the three claims set out earlier have been adequately demonstrated: that gods exist, that they are careful, and that they are wholly not to be turned aside against justice; Clinias agrees."
limits: This records the argumentative closure of the three theological claims. It does not include the later statutory reporting procedure.
review_status: accepted
```

The first officials who hear must bring the case to the appointed court, and an official who fails to act becomes liable to an impiety charge."
textual_basis: "At 907c-907e, the Athenian explains that the forceful prelude aimed to keep bad people from thinking argumentative victory gives them license to do whatever they want concerning gods, and that if the prelude has even slightly persuaded them to hate themselves and love opposite characters, it has been well spoken. He then says a post-prelude speech should rightly interpret the laws by ordering impious people to change to pious ways. For those not persuaded, he states the law: if someone is impious in speech or deed, a bystander must report to officials; the first officials who hear must bring the case to the appointed court according to the laws; an official who hears and fails to act is liable to prosecution for impiety."
limits: This records the transition from prelude to the first reporting and liability rule. It does not include the specific penalty scale after conviction beyond the court's role in assessing a penalty.
review_status: accepted

textual_basis: At 908b-908e, the speaker first describes a person who does not believe in gods but naturally has a just character, hates bad people, avoids injustice, and loves just people. limits: This records the taxonomy of atheistic impiety by character and harm. It does not claim that every seer, commander, or sophist is included in the harmful class.

The court is to sentence them to the middle-country prison with no free-person access, regulated food from slaves, unburied expulsion after death, impiety liability for a free person who helps bury them, and orphan care for their children.
limits: This records the legal handling of the manipulative offender class. It does not state a general rule for all ritual specialists, include the less malicious correction track before this span, or include the public-cult rule that begins at the end of 909d.

observation: Sale or purchase exchanges receive legal protection only when delivery occurs in the assigned market place and the price is received immediately. Sales or purchases made elsewhere, otherwise, or on postponement are treated as trust-based dealings without statutory actions for nonconforming sales.
textual_basis: At 915d-915e, the rule requires giving and receiving in the place appointed for each market and receiving the price at once; it forbids sale or purchase elsewhere and on postponement, and says a person who exchanges otherwise acts as though no legal actions exist for sales not made under the stated terms.

english_gloss: enslaved person, sacred disease, doctor, trainer, six months, year, double
observation: The return action for selling an enslaved person with a long, hard-to-cure bodily or mental disease is limited by buyer expertise, disclosure, disease type, and seller status. A physician or trainer buyer has no return action, nor does a buyer who was told the truth. When a craftsman sells such a person to a private buyer, the buyer has six months to return, except for the sacred disease where the period is one year; selected doctors judge the case, and the losing seller pays double the price. For a private seller to a private buyer, the same return and judgment procedure applies, but the losing seller pays the price only once.
textual_basis: At 916a-916c, the law lists several concealed or difficult diseases, exempts physician and trainer buyers and truthful disclosure, sets six-month and one-year return periods, assigns adjudication to selected doctors, and then distinguishes double repayment from simple repayment according to seller status.
limits: This observation is limited to the specified return action for the listed disease cases. It does not state a general warranty rule for every sale of an enslaved person.
review_status: rejected
```

textual_basis: At 916c-916d, the rule denies return when a knowing seller sells to a knowing buyer, grants return when a buyer did not know and later perceives the fact, assigns judgment to the five youngest law-guardians, and adds house purification plus triple repayment for a seller found to have known.

It then introduces a prelude, groups counterfeiting with falsehood and deception, criticizes leaving occasion, place, and time unordered and undefined, and states that the lawgiver must always make greater or smaller limits clear.

textual_basis: At 917a-917c, the passage ranks false oath-taking and lying before superiors, says the market counterfeiter lies and deceives while invoking gods under market-warden rules, then states the law against two prices, same-day repricing, praise, and oaths, with the bystander striking rule for a citizen of at least thirty.

observation: The counterfeit-goods rule assigns both disclosure duties and status-specific consequences. A knowledgeable person able to expose the counterfeit must do so before officials; a slave or metic who exposes it carries off the counterfeit item, while a citizen who does not expose it is publicly condemned as depriving the gods and a citizen who does expose it dedicates it to the gods of the market. textual_basis: At 917c-917e, the law addresses the person selling counterfeit goods, requires knowledgeable exposure before officials, differentiates slave, metic, and citizen outcomes, then adds deprivation of the counterfeit item and a lash-per-drachma punishment proclaimed by a herald.

textual_basis: At 918c-918e, the Athenian asks why useful commercial activities appear shameful and says the matter needs no small virtue. He contrasts a rare nature trained by excellent nurture, which can hold to measure when large profits are possible, with the many, who need without measure and choose profit greedily. This contrast is used to explain why the commercial occupations have fallen under shameful reproaches.
limits: This does not say the occupations are intrinsically bad. The passage explicitly keeps their useful function in view while locating the disgrace in common conduct around gain.

textual_basis: "At 919b-919d, the Athenian says the lawgiver must always cut out a remedy for the abuses just described, compares the problem to fighting two opposed things as in diseases, and identifies the two opponents as poverty and wealth. He then lists three responses: minimize reliance on retailers, assign the work to people whose corruption would not greatly harm the city, and devise a means so the practitioners do not easily acquire shameless and unfree habits."

It then assigns judgment of the free and unfree to those who have received the prizes of excellence, allows anyone to bring a charge of familial shame, and sets one year of bonds for the first conviction with later terms doubled.

observation: The wage-contract law treats craft value as something the craftsman knows and should not manipulate through bargaining tricks in a free city. If a hirer fails to pay wages according to the lawful agreement, the law protects the city's bond with the gods by requiring double payment and, after a year, a monthly surcharge, with suits in tribal courts.
textual_basis: At 921b-921d, the Athenian says the seller had been advised not to test for a higher price but to price simply according to value, and the same is ordered for the buyer, since the craftsman knows the value. He says a craftsman should not practice deceptive craft against private persons in free cities, and that the wronged person has suits against the wrongdoer. He then states that one who receives work in advance and does not pay the wages at the agreed times must be charged double; if a year passes, he pays an added monthly amount per drachma, and the suits belong in the tribal courts.
limits: This records the ordinary craft-wage rule and its penalties. It does not include the later advisory rule about military public service.

observation: The discussion extends the craftsman category to people whose technical work preserves the city in war, including generals and military specialists. For those who complete public work well, the corresponding payment is honor, and the law is framed as mixed with praise and advisory rather than coercive.
textual_basis: At 921d-922a, the Athenian says that, because craftsmen have been mentioned, it is fair to add a side remark about craftsmen of wartime preservation, generals and others technical in these matters. If one of them undertakes public work, willingly or by proper order, and completes it well, the city should pay the honors that are the wages of military men. If such a person receives a noble military work in advance and does not return it, the law will blame him; the law is to be set down mixed with praise, advisory and not compulsory, telling the multitude to honor good men who save the city through courage or military devices.
limits: This records the honor-payment frame for military public service. It does not include the following transition to orphan and inheritance arrangements.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: contracts, orphan matters, guardians, to die, disposition, having disposed, unordered, laws, characters, will
observation: After the main contracts have been arranged, the Athenian marks orphan matters and guardianship as still necessary and difficult. He says wills cannot be left unordered, because unrestricted testamentary power would let people set down many divergent and mutually opposed arrangements, conflicting with law, with the characters of the living, and even with their own earlier dispositions before facing death.
textual_basis: "At 922a-922c, the Athenian says the greatest mutual contracts have almost been ordered except for orphan matters and guardians' care of orphans, which must now be arranged. He names the starting points as the desires of those about to die concerning disposition and the fortunes of those who have made no disposition. Looking to the difficulty, he says the matter cannot be left unordered: if a will made in any condition near life's end were simply authoritative, each person would lay down many things different from and opposed to one another, to the laws, to the characters of the living, and to their own earlier selves."
limits: This records why testamentary law is introduced. It does not yet include the quoted complaint of the dying person or the specific statutory inheritance rules.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: to die, speech, lawgivers, master, anger, it will be permitted, bad, good, tested, legislating
observation: The dying person's case for free disposition is presented as an angry demand for mastery over all property. The argument appeals to personal testing of who proved good or bad in sickness, old age, and other events; the Athenian answers that earlier lawgivers who yielded to this speech were soft and looked only narrowly at human affairs.
textual_basis: At 922c-922e, Clinias asks how the problem is difficult, and the Athenian says a human being about to die is difficult and full of a speech very fearful and troublesome for lawgivers. The dying person, seeking to be master of everything, says it is terrible if he cannot give or withhold his own property as he wishes, assigning more or less to those around him after they have been tested in sickness, old age, and many fortunes. When Clinias asks whether they speak well, the Athenian says earlier lawgivers were soft and legislated while looking only at a small part of human affairs.
limits: This records the rhetorical pressure for testamentary freedom and the criticism of yielding to it. It does not include the legislator's positive ownership principle that follows.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The legislator's reply denies simple self-ownership and simple private ownership at the point of death. Persons and property are said to belong to the whole lineage, past and future, and still more to the city; therefore the lawgiver will not let illness, old age, or flattery redirect dispositions against what is best for the city and the family.
textual_basis: "At 923a-923b, the Athenian says he and Clinias will answer those about to die more fittingly: as creatures of a day, they have difficulty knowing their own property and themselves, as the Pythian inscription says. Speaking as lawgiver, he says he does not set them down as belonging to themselves, nor the estate as theirs, but as belonging to their whole family, before and after, and still more as both the family and estate belonging to the city. On this basis he says he will not willingly allow someone, by flatteries during illness or unstable old age, to persuade them to dispose contrary to the best, but will legislate looking to what is best for the whole city and family."
limits: This records the ownership principle behind the will law. It does not include the detailed statutory allocation among sons, daughters, adopted heirs, and guardians.
review_status: accepted
```

  - κληρονόμον
  - κλήρῳ
  - ἀποικίαν
  - πατρῴου
  - οἶκος
  - θυγατρί
  - καταλειπέτω
english_gloss: consolations, preludes, will, heir, allotment, colony, ancestral, household, daughter, let him leave
observation: The law following the testamentary prelude gives a father limited choices rather than unrestricted disposition. He writes one son as heir, records children given for adoption, may give surplus property to sons not assigned to an allotment and expected to be sent to a colony, withholds shares from sons who already have a household and from betrothed daughters, and if no males remain may leave a daughter's husband as his son and heir.
textual_basis: "At 923c-923e, after calling the preceding words consolations and preludes for the living and dying, the Athenian states the law: a father writing a will first writes as heir whichever son he deems worthy, and records any other child he gives to another to adopt. If a son remains not made upon an allotment and is legally expected to be sent to a colony, the father may give him as much as he wishes from the remaining property except the ancestral allotment and its equipment; if there are several, he divides surplus as he wishes. He should not assign money to a son who already has a household, nor to a daughter already betrothed, but should assign to an unbetrothed daughter. If after the will a local allotment appears for a son or daughter, it is left to the heir; if there are no males but daughters, he writes as heir the husband of whichever daughter he wishes, leaving him as his son."
limits: This records the main testamentary allocation rules for a father. It does not include the backup naming of a substitute child if an adopted or natural son dies young, or the guardianship rules.
review_status: accepted
```

textual_basis: At 924a-924b, the Athenian turns to cases where children need guardians. If the deceased has written willing guardians who agree to serve, the written selection is authoritative. If someone dies without a will or with the guardian selection incomplete, the guardians are the nearest authoritative kin, two from the father's side, two from the mother's side, and one from the dead person's friends, whom the law-guardians install for the orphan in need.
limits: This records guardian appointment by will and kinship fallback. It does not include the preceding substitute-child and childless-adoption provisions, or the continuation of guardianship supervision after this span.

textual_basis: At 928a-928b, the law is described as both encouraging and threatening about orphan legislation. observation: The orphan-guardianship law distributes enforcement across officials, guardians, relatives, citizens, and the grown orphan. Penalties include double assessment against an official in the selected court, quadruple payment by a culpable guardian split between the child and prosecutor, a five-year window for the former orphan to sue, and removal of a law-guardian who harms the orphan unjustly.
textual_basis: At 928b-928d, an official may penalize a guardian who acts contrary to the law, while a guardian may bring the official into the selected court for a double assessment. If relatives or any citizen think a guardian is neglectful or doing wrong, they may bring him to the same court; a conviction requires quadruple payment, half to the child and half to the successful prosecutor. After reaching youth, an orphan may bring a guardianship suit within five years after the guardianship ends. If an official harms the orphan through neglect, the court assesses payment to the child; if through injustice, he is removed from the office of law-guardian and replaced by the city.
limits: This records the enforcement machinery for orphan guardianship. It does not cover the later law about father-son severance except where the cited span begins to transition after the orphan rule.

observation: The discussion introduces extreme father-child disputes as cases where fathers want legal power to disown sons and sons want power to bring madness charges against fathers. In this city, a disowned child must emigrate because the fixed number of households admits no additional household, so the law requires severance by the whole kin-group rather than by one father alone.
textual_basis: At 928d-929a, the Athenian says disputes between fathers and children can exceed what is needed, with fathers wanting authority to publicly renounce a son and sons wanting authority to prosecute fathers for madness when disease or old age has made them behave shamefully. He says such things arise in very bad characters, and that in another regime a disowned child would not necessarily be without a city. In the present regime the fatherless person must settle in another land because no one may be added to the five thousand and forty households; therefore the person about to suffer this must be renounced in legal process by the whole kin-group, not by one father.
limits: This records the rationale for requiring kin-group process in disowning. It does not include all procedural voting requirements, which are stated in the following span.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: anger, relatives, cousins, mother, let him accuse, speeches, fellow voters, disown
observation: A father who wants to sever a son from his kinship may not do it immediately or lightly. He must gather his own relatives up to cousins and the son's maternal relatives, make his accusation before them, allow the son equal speeches in reply, and obtain more than half of the adult relatives' votes, excluding the father, mother, and accused son from the vote.
textual_basis: At 929a-929c, the law says that if anger, whether justified or not, leads a father to desire to remove the son he begot and raised from his kinship, it must not be permitted easily or at once. First he must collect his relatives up to cousins and likewise the son's relatives on the mother's side. He accuses before them, teaching that the son deserves expulsion from the kin-group, and gives the son equal speeches to show he deserves none of this. If the father persuades them and gains more than half the votes of all adult relatives, with father, mother, and accused son excluded, then and only then may he disown the son.
limits: This records the hearing and voting threshold for disowning. It does not include the later adoption and colony fallback for a disowned son.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: Remarriage after a spouse's death is differentiated by the sufficiency of existing children and by the surviving spouse. A widow with enough children remains and raises them, while a younger healthy widow is handled through relatives and the marriage women, especially if children are lacking.
textual_basis: From 930b through 930d the law separates the case of a wife dying from that of a husband dying, marks one rule as advisory rather than compulsory, ties compulsory remarriage to lack of children, and defines exact child sufficiency as one male and one female.

review_status: accepted

The passage adds that the nature of such things is not easy to know or to persuade others about, and it names wax images placed at doors, crossroads, and parental tombs as cases where simple dismissal is not persuasive without a clear doctrine.

A convicted doctor who poisons for nonlethal human harm or for harm to animals or hives is punished by death, while a private person has the penalty assessed by the court; the same pattern is applied to binding, spell, or incantation cases by assigning death to a seer or omen-reader and court assessment to a non-specialist.
textual_basis: "At 933d-933e, the law states that if someone uses drugs for nonfatal harm to a person, or for harm to livestock or hives, a doctor convicted of the drug case is to be punished by death, while the court assesses what a private person should suffer or pay. It then turns to bindings, spells, incantations, and similar poisonings: if the convicted person is a seer or omen-reader, he is to die, while the one without divination again receives court assessment of suffering or payment."
limits: This records the penalty distinction based on professional or ritual expertise. It does not cover lethal human poisonings, which the passage says had already been stated elsewhere.
review_status: accepted
```

Compensation is to match the harm until the injured matter is healed, while the extra penalty is lighter for wrongdoing through another's folly or youthful persuasion and heavier for wrongdoing from the agent's own folly, lack of self-control, fear, desire, envy, or hard-to-cure anger. The stated aim is future correction, not undoing the past event, and the judge is described as helping the lawgiver when a law leaves penalty assessment to the court.

Each wrongdoing also receives a corrective penalty: the passage distinguishes lighter and heavier causes, states that punishment is not paid because the deed can become undone, and gives future aims such as hating injustice or easing the condition. It then says the judge must assist the lawgiver when the law entrusts the assessment of what the defendant must suffer or pay."
limits: This records the general penalty theory attached to theft and violence. It does not supply the later itemized penalties for every particular theft or violent act.
review_status: accepted

It therefore bans such speech in sanctuaries, public sacrifices, games, marketplace, court, and any common assembly, and makes the relevant official responsible for punishing it or losing any claim to distinction for neglect of law.
textual_basis: At 935b-935c, the Athenian says people in such situations often utter something ridiculous about the opposite party, and that habitual practice of this makes one miss the serious way or lose much of high-mindedness. For this reason nobody is to utter such things in a sanctuary, public sacrifices, games, marketplace, court, or common meeting. Each official over these matters must punish without liability, or else never compete for distinctions because he does not care for the laws or do what the lawgiver commanded.

He then states that a maker of comedy, iambs, or musical song may in no way comicize any citizen, by word or image, angrily or not. If someone disobeys, the contest judges must drive him from the country the same day or pay three minas sacred to the god whose contest it is.

textual_basis: "At 936b-936c, the Athenian says the pitiable person is not simply someone hungry or similarly afflicted, but a moderate person, or someone with virtue or part of it, who also has some misfortune. He says it would be astonishing if such a person were entirely neglected into the last poverty in a moderately governed city. Therefore the lawgiver may safely set a law: no beggar is to come into being in the city. If someone attempts this by gathering a life with ineffective prayers, market officials remove him from the market, city officials from the town, and rural officials send him from the rest of the country to the border so the land is wholly clean of such a creature."

observation: Damage by a slave is assigned to the master unless the injured party helped cause it through ignorance or unreasonable use. The master must fully repair the damage or surrender the slave; if he alleges a collusive trick to deprive him of the slave, the dispute is tried as bad craft, with double slave value awarded if he wins, while animals that damage neighbors are handled by the same compensation rule.
textual_basis: At 936c-936e, the Athenian says if a male or female slave damages another person's property, without the injured party being partly responsible through ignorance or some unwise use, the master of the damaging slave must either cure the damage fully or hand over the slave. If the master accuses the injured party of a joint trick with the slave to deprive him of the slave, he is to litigate bad craft against the claimant; if he wins he receives double the value of the slave as assessed by the court, and if he loses he repairs the damage and hands over the slave. The same payment rule applies when a pack animal, horse, dog, or other livestock injures a neighbor's property.
limits: This records liability for slaves and animals causing damage. It does not include later witness rules.
review_status: accepted

One called as a witness who does not meet the caller is liable for the damage. A witness raised by a judge does not vote in that case. A free woman may testify and advocate if over forty, and may bring a suit if without a husband; if her husband is alive she may testify only. A female slave, male slave, or child may testify and advocate only for homicide, if a reliable guarantor is provided that the person will remain until trial if accused of false testimony.

observation: False testimony rules allow either litigant to challenge all or part of testimony before the case is decided, with sealed objections preserved for later adjudication. A twice-convicted false witness is no longer compelled to testify, a thrice-convicted one may not testify and faces death if he does, and cases won by a majority of testimony later convicted as false can be reopened through a further proceeding.
textual_basis: At 937b-937d, each litigant may object to all or part of testimony before judgment if he claims someone testified falsely; officials keep the sealed objections from both parties for the judgment on false testimony. If someone is twice convicted of false testimony, no law compels him to testify; if three times, he is no longer permitted to testify, and if he dares to testify after three convictions anyone may denounce him to the official, who hands him to a court, with death as the penalty if convicted. If testimonies convicted as false seemed to have produced victory for the successful party, and more than half such testimonies are condemned, the case lost on these testimonies becomes subject to retrial and dispute over whether it was decided by them; however that issue is decided, it settles the earlier suits.
limits: This records false-witness objection, disqualification, capital sanction, and retrial mechanism. It does not include the following critique of corrupt legal advocacy.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The prelude to advocacy law praises justice as something that has civilized human life and treats assisting in lawsuits as potentially noble. It then identifies a corrupt art that defames this good name by claiming a device for litigating and co-advocating that can win whether the case is just or not, and that can sell its speeches for money.
textual_basis: At 937d-938a, the Athenian says many fine things in human life have destructive contaminations growing upon them, and asks how justice among humans is not fine since it has tamed all human affairs. If justice is fine, co-advocacy would also be fine. But a certain badness slanders these things by attaching the fine name of craft to itself; it claims to be a device of lawsuits, able both to litigate and advocate for another and to win whether the matters in the case have been justly or unjustly done, and it gives the craft and its speeches as a gift in exchange for money.
limits: This records the diagnosis of corrupt advocacy as victory-oriented and saleable. It does not include the statutory penalties that follow.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: craft, experience, justice, just things, judges, litigate excessively, bad litigation, bad advocacy, love of money, love of victory
observation: "The law tries to prevent a victory-oriented advocacy practice from arising in the city; anyone suspected of turning judges away from the power of just things, litigating excessively, or advocating badly is tried in the selected court. Penalties are assessed by motive: love of victory leads to a timed ban from suing or advocating, while love of money brings exile or death for a foreigner and death for a citizen, and a second conviction for love of victory also becomes capital."
textual_basis: At 938a-938c, the Athenian says that whether this practice is a craft or an unartful experience and habit, it especially must not arise in the city; if it exists, the lawgiver asks it to obey and not speak contrary to justice, but depart elsewhere. For those who disobey, the law says anyone may indict a person who seems to try to turn the power of just things in judges' souls toward the opposite, litigate out of season over such matters, or co-advocate badly; he is tried in the court of selected judges. If convicted, the court assesses whether he acts from love of money or love of victory. For love of victory, the court sets how long he may not bring suit or advocate; for love of money, a foreigner must leave and never return or die, while a citizen dies for honoring gain from every direction; if twice judged to act this way from love of victory, he dies.
limits: This records the bad-litigation and bad-advocacy penalty law. It does not include earlier witness procedure except as part of the larger procedural sequence.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: theft, seizure, slavish, shameless, Zeus, sons, poets, myth-tellers, true, likely, lawgiver
observation: The theft prelude labels theft as slavish and seizure as shameless, then rejects the idea that divine models authorize deceit or force. It warns hearers not to be misled by poets or myth-tellers into thinking such acts are acceptable because gods do them, and says the lawgiver is more competent than the poets on this point.
textual_basis: At 941b-941c, the passage calls theft slavish and seizure shameless, says none of the sons of Zeus has practiced either deceit or force with pleasure, and tells people not to be deceived by poets or other faulty myth-tellers into believing that theft or violence is not shameful because gods do such things. It adds that this is neither true nor likely, and that knowing this belongs more to the lawgiver than to all the poets.
limits: This records the explicit prelude to the theft law. It does not infer a general theory of poetry or theology beyond the stated warning about using divine stories to excuse theft or force.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: public property, large, small, stealing, desire, capacity, curable, incurable, foreigner, slave, citizen, fatherland, death
observation: "For theft of public property, the law treats large and small thefts as belonging to the same kind of case, because the smaller thief has the same desire with less capacity. Penalty is not scaled simply by the size of the theft but by whether the offender is curable: a foreigner or slave convicted of public theft receives court-assessed penalty, while a citizen who plunders or violently seizes from the fatherland is punished by death as nearly incurable."
textual_basis: At 941c-942a, the law says that anyone stealing something public, large or small, needs the same justice, because the small thief has stolen with the same desire but less power, and the larger thief has moved the greater thing unjustly. It says the law does not punish either because of the lesser or greater size of the theft, but because one may still be curable and the other incurable. It then assigns court assessment to a foreigner or slave caught stealing public property, but death to a citizen, raised as he is expected to have been raised, who is caught plundering or violently seizing the fatherland, whether caught in the act or not.
limits: This records the stated penalty distinction for public theft. It does not cover private theft or every later military-law consequence in the following section.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The military section makes absence of command the chief thing to avoid for both males and females. It requires habituation against acting alone, even in play, and presents war and peace alike as training people to look toward a ruler, follow commands in ordinary routines and danger, and live as much as possible in gathered, simultaneous, common action.
textual_basis: At 942a-942d, the passage says the greatest military rule is that no one should ever be without rule, whether male or female, and that no soul should be habituated to do anything by itself alone, either in serious activity or in play. It lists ordinary commanded actions such as standing, marching, exercising, bathing, eating, and waking for guard duties, and says that in danger no one should pursue or retreat without the commanders' indication. It sums this up as teaching the soul neither to know nor understand acting apart from the others, but to make life gathered, simultaneous, and common as much as possible, and to practice ruling and being ruled from childhood.
limits: This records the military discipline program within the passage. It does not claim that every civic activity outside this military context is governed by the same rule.
review_status: accepted

observation: A person enrolled or assigned to military service must serve, and absence through cowardice without release by generals is tried as nonservice before the military authorities when they return from camp. The judges are those who actually served, divided by military class, and conviction bars the offender from future contests for overall military excellence, from accusing another of nonservice, and from acting as prosecutor in such cases, while leaving further penalty to the court.
textual_basis: "At 943a-943b, the law says that the enrolled person or the person assigned to some part must serve. If someone leaves out through cowardice without the generals releasing him, charges of nonservice go to the military officials when they return from camp. Each class of those who served judges separately: hoplites judge hoplites, horsemen judge horsemen, and the others likewise judge their own military associates. If someone is convicted, he may never become a contestant for overall excellence, never write up another for nonservice, and never be prosecutor about these matters; the court also assesses what he must suffer or pay."
limits: This records the nonservice procedure and disabilities. It does not cover the separate award process that follows after these trials.
review_status: accepted

textual_basis: At 943b-943c, once the nonservice suits have been judged, the officers of each group are to make an assembly again, and anyone wishing to be judged for excellence does so among his own groups. english_gloss: laying-out, processions, tombs, white, laments, wailings, chorus, hymn, praise, martial
observation: The funeral for successful auditors is separated from ordinary citizen funerals by ritual color, song, and procession. The law prescribes white clothing, excludes laments and wailing, surrounds the bier with male and female choruses singing praise through the day, and sends youths, unmarried men in martial equipment, boys, girls, and post-childbearing women in ordered procession.
textual_basis: At 947b-947d, the passage says the laying-out, procession, and burial are to differ from those of other citizens. It requires all-white dress, no laments or wailing, two choruses around the bier singing praise and blessing through the day, and a morning procession with one hundred gymnasium youths carrying the bier, martial ranks going before, boys singing an ancestral song near the bier, and girls and older women following behind.
limits: This records the funeral procession and praise elements. It does not include the later underground tomb construction or annual contests, which are described in the following span.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: oaths, litigants, accusations, denial, unsworn, perjured, judge, gain
observation: The oath law removes oaths from profit-bearing litigation while retaining oaths for offices where perjury offers no obvious gain. Plaintiffs and defendants write accusations and denials without oath, because frequent lawsuits would otherwise create widespread perjury among people who continue to share civic and private life; by contrast, judges, public office selectors, sacred voters, and contest officials may still use oaths where human opinion sees no profit in perjury.
textual_basis: "At 948d-949a, the passage says intelligent lawgivers should remove oaths from both litigants at the conclusion of lawsuits: the accuser writes charges without adding an oath, and the defendant submits a written denial unsworn. It gives the reason that in a city with many lawsuits nearly half the people would knowingly be perjured while still mixing in common meals and private associations. The next law keeps oaths for judges, those establishing public offices, sacred voting, and contest officials in music, gymnastic, and equestrian matters, but says cases where denial and swearing appear to bring large gain are to be judged without judicial oaths between litigants."
limits: This records the contrast between retained public oaths and excluded litigant oaths. It does not include the continuation of the sentence after the assigned 949a span.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: "The approved young observers become special objects of civic surveillance: the city honors those who turn out well and dishonors failures more sharply than others. A returning traveler who has observed foreign customs must report any findings about laws, education, or nurture to the whole council; if he returns improved he is praised and honored, but if corrupted he is barred from social influence and can be executed if he meddles with education and laws after disobeying officials."
textual_basis: At 952b-952d, the Athenian says the whole city must watch approved young men, honor those who succeed, and dishonor those who turn out worse than the many. One who has observed customs among other peoples must immediately go to the council and share any report about lawmaking, education, or nurture, or anything he himself has noticed. If he appears neither worse nor better he is praised for zeal, if much better he receives greater praise while alive and fitting honors after death, and if corrupted he must not associate with young or old while pretending wisdom. If he obeys officials he lives privately; if not, and if convicted in court of meddling with education and laws, he dies.
limits: This records the screening of returning civic observers. It does not include the subsequent classification of incoming foreigners.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: "The visitor laws culminate in reciprocal exchange: the rare philosophical visitor teaches and learns, then departs as a friend honored by friends with suitable gifts and honors. The city must receive foreign men and women and send out its own under these laws, honoring Zeus of strangers without practicing food-and-sacrifice expulsions or savage proclamations."
textual_basis: At 953d-953e, the Athenian says the rare observer should associate with the education official or virtue-victor, teach some things and learn others, and depart as a friend from friends, honored with fitting gifts and honors. He then says all foreign men and women from another country are to be received, and the city's own sent out, according to these laws, honoring Zeus of strangers, not making exclusions by foods and sacrifices as the Nile herds do now, nor by savage proclamations.
limits: This records the xenia closure to the visitor laws. It does not include the following guarantee and search statutes.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: A person who wants to search another's premises must first swear by the lawful gods that he expects to find the item, and must search naked or in an ungirt tunic. Refusal to permit search creates double-damage liability, while searches during the householder's absence distinguish unsealed items, short sealed custody, and longer absence requiring city officials to open and reseal sealed things.
textual_basis: At 954a-954c, the Athenian says anyone who wants to search with someone must do so naked or wearing an ungirt tunic after first swearing by the lawful gods that he expects to find the object; the other person must provide the house, both sealed and unsealed items, for search. If someone does not allow a searcher to search, the excluded person may sue after valuing the item sought, and a convicted person pays double the assessed damage. If the householder is away, residents provide unsealed items for search; sealed items are sealed over and a guardian appointed for five days by the searcher. If the householder is away longer, the searcher takes the city officials, opens sealed things, and then reseals them in the same way with the household members and city officials.
limits: This records search procedure for suspected property. It does not include the time limits for disputed possession that follow.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: The law sets limitation periods after which disputed movable possessions may no longer be challenged, while land and houses in this city are excluded from such dispute. Public visible use in city, market, or temples becomes unchallengeable after a year; visible rural use after five years; household use in town after three years; hidden rural possession after ten; and possession abroad has no time limit once found.
textual_basis: At 954c-954e, the Athenian gives a time limit for disputable things after which possession may no longer be challenged. He says there is no such dispute about lands and dwellings here. For other things, if someone is seen using what he possesses in city, market, and temples, and no one lays claim while another says he is seeking it, if a year passes the possession may not be challenged. If it is not used in city or market but openly in the fields and no claimant appears within five years, after five years it may no longer be challenged. If someone uses it in houses in town, the limit is three years; if possessed hidden in the fields, ten years; if in another country, there is no time limit on laying claim whenever it is discovered.
limits: This records property-claim limitation periods. It does not include forceful obstruction of lawsuits or contests.
review_status: accepted

observation: Forcefully preventing someone or witnesses from attending a trial voids the proceeding when a slave is blocked, and for a free person also brings a year of imprisonment plus liability to an enslavement charge. Forcefully blocking an athletic, musical, or other competitor requires contest officials to free the entrant; if they cannot and the blocker wins, the prizes and victory inscription are transferred to the blocked competitor, and the blocker remains liable for damages whether he wins or loses.
textual_basis: At 954e-955b, the Athenian says if someone forcefully prevents another from appearing in a suit, whether the person himself or witnesses, then if the blocked person is a slave, one's own or another's, the suit becomes incomplete and invalid; if a free person is blocked, besides invalidity the blocker is imprisoned for a year and becomes liable to anyone who wishes for enslavement. If someone forcefully prevents a rival in gymnastics, music, or another contest from appearing, anyone may report it to the contest judges, who are to release the would-be competitor into the contest. If they cannot, and the blocker wins, the prizes are to be given to the blocked competitor and he is to be inscribed as victor in any temples he wishes; the blocker may make no dedication or inscription for that contest and is liable for damage whether he loses or wins.
limits: This records forceful obstruction of trials and contests. It does not include receiving stolen goods or private war and peace.
review_status: accepted
```

observation: "Private suits are organized as a three-stage sequence: party-chosen arbitral judges first, village and tribal panels second, and selected judges third, with added monetary stakes for litigants who press beyond earlier decisions."
textual_basis: At 956b-956e, after the laws on contracts have been stated, the remaining business is said to be lawsuits. The first court consists of judges jointly chosen by defendant and prosecutor and is more aptly called arbitration. If they do not decide the matter, the second stage goes to village and tribal panels, with the defendant paying a fifth of the assessed amount after a second loss. A third contest goes to selected judges; repeated loss brings the defendant one-and-a-half times the assessed amount, while a prosecutor who continues after losing faces either a fifth at the second stage or half the assessment at the third.
limits: This records the appeal ladder and attached payment risks. It does not cover the later administrative details of court lots, timings, voting, postponements, answers, or deposits.
review_status: accepted

The laying-out is not to be indoors longer than the time that shows both the apparently dead person and the truly dead person, and third-day removal to the tomb is set as a fitting human measure.
limits: This records external funeral display limits. It does not include the soul-body rationale that follows.
review_status: accepted
```

The discussion turns to the names of the Fates and especially the irreversible power associated with Atropos, and asks how such power must come to the laws according to nature. Clinias urges not leaving until this is secured for the stated laws.
limits: This records the transition from completed statutes to the problem of preserving the laws. It does not identify the preserving institution, which begins in the next marker.
review_status: accepted

limits: This records a stated method for precise inquiry. It does not identify the one form in this passage before the subsequent virtue discussion.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: astronomy, atheists, necessities, acts of thought, soulless things, intellect, soul, atheisms
observation: The closing discussion reverses the common suspicion that astronomy and its allied arts make practitioners atheistic. The harmful form of the study is traced to treating heavenly motions as necessities without purposive thought and to treating the visible heavens as soulless bodies that assign causes to the cosmos.
textual_basis: "At 967a-967d the Athenian reports that many suppose astronomy and the necessary arts connected with it make people atheistic because such students see events as produced by necessities rather than by deliberative purposes concerning goods. He then says the present position is the opposite: earlier investigators wondered how soulless bodies could use such exact calculations, some dared to say intellect orders the heavens, but the same people erred by making soul younger than bodies, with the result that the visible heavenly things appeared full of stone, earth, and other soulless bodies distributing the causes of the cosmos. He identifies that earlier account as producing many atheisms, difficulties, and poetic abuse of philosophers."
limits: This records the diagnostic reversal about astronomy and atheism. It does not yet state the positive educational requirements for rulers.
review_status: accepted
```

english_gloss: laws, to legislate, teaching, association, list, ages, studies, due moment
observation: The Athenian denies that the decisive details of the nocturnal council can yet be legislated in writing. The institution must be constructed through teaching and much association, beginning with a list of suitable people by age, learning capacity, character, and habit; written schedules of what and when to learn are called useless before knowledge of the timely moment arises in the learner's soul.
textual_basis: At 968c-968e the Athenian says it is no longer possible to legislate laws about such matters before the council has been ordered; only then will the members legislate authoritatively about what they must govern. For now, what constructs such things would come through teaching with much association if it comes correctly. He says first a list must be drawn of those suited to the guard by age, powers for learning, character, and habits. He adds that what must be learned is hard to discover and hard to learn from another, and that writing down the times and occasions for each item is vain, since the learners themselves would not know that it is being learned at the right moment until knowledge has come to be inside each soul.
limits: This records the stated non-written and association-based formation process. It does not infer a general doctrine about all writing.
review_status: accepted
```

He says he will share the risk by speaking and explaining what seems established to him about the education and nurture now stirred again by the arguments, while adding that the danger is not small and not suited for just anyone. He then urges Clinias to care for this, since by correctly constructing the city of the Magnesians, or whatever name the god gives it, he will win the greatest renown or at least never avoid seeming the bravest among later generations.

observation: The orphan legislation distinguishes daily way of life from civic treatment. The Athenian says special guardianship laws would make sense if orphan life needed private practices very different from non-orphan life, but in this city orphanhood is not very different from life under paternal law in such matters; what cannot be equalized is its treatment through honors, dishonors, and forms of care.
textual_basis: At 927e the Athenian says that if they lacked moderately stated laws about these same matters, there would be reason to set down special guardianship laws as greatly different and to diversify orphan life with private practices beside that of non-orphans. review_status: accepted

textual_basis: The question at 639c specifies a praiser or blamer of an association and contrasts correct association under a ruler with experience only of leaderless or badly ruled cases; the reply at 639d denies competence to those who have never seen or shared in a correct example.
limits: The record is limited to the stated criterion for useful praise or blame in 639c-639d and does not infer the truth of any later claims about drinking parties.
review_status: accepted
```
